blocks.html: In Collision Theory and Reaction Rate you saw why reactions speed up when particles collide more often and harder. Now we put a number on "how fast." Concentrations are in moles per liter (molarity), so a rate is a change in molarity per unit of time, usually $\text{M/s}$.

For $a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \to c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}$, the rate of reaction is
$$\text{rate} = -\frac{1}{a}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{A}]}{\Delta t} = -\frac{1}{b}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{B}]}{\Delta t}$$ $$= \frac{1}{c}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{C}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{d}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{D}]}{\Delta t}$$
It is always positive, and every substance gives the same value.

Reactant concentrations fall, so $\Delta[\mathrm{A}]$ is negative. The minus sign turns it into a positive rate. The coefficients matter because the equation fixes the ratio in which things are used and made. In $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3}$, hydrogen disappears three times as fast as nitrogen, because three $\mathrm{H_2}$ react for every $\mathrm{N_2}$. Dividing each change by its coefficient removes that difference, so the reaction has one rate, no matter which substance you watch.

A rate measured between two times is an average rate. Rates usually slow down as reactants are used up, so the rate at one moment, the instantaneous rate, is the slope of the tangent to the concentration curve at that time (with a minus sign for a reactant). The initial rate is the instantaneous rate at $t = 0$, before products build up.

blocks.cap: Drag the point along the curve. The tangent's slope is the instantaneous rate; it is steepest at the start and flattens as the reactant runs down.

blocks.title: One rate for the whole reaction
blocks.q: In $\mathrm{2N_2O_5 \to 4NO_2 + O_2}$, $[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]$ falls from $0.0200\ \text{M}$ to $0.0170\ \text{M}$ in $100\ \text{s}$. Find the rate at which $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$ is used, the rate of reaction, and the rates at which $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ form.
steps: Rate of reaction: divide by its coefficient, 2: $\tfrac{1}{2}(3.0 \times 10^{-5}) = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M/s}$.
$\mathrm{NO_2}$ has coefficient 4: it forms at $4(1.5 \times 10^{-5}) = 6.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M/s}$. $\mathrm{O_2}$ has coefficient 1: $1.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M/s}$.

blocks.title: Working from a product
blocks.q: In $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3}$, ammonia forms at $0.060\ \text{M/s}$. How fast is $\mathrm{H_2}$ used?
steps: $\mathrm{H_2}$ has coefficient 3: $3(0.030) = 0.090\ \text{M/s}$. Its concentration falls, so $\Delta[\mathrm{H_2}]/\Delta t = -0.090\ \text{M/s}$, but the rate is reported as a positive number.

blocks.html: Reporting a reactant's rate as a negative number, or comparing rates of different substances without the coefficients. The rate is positive by definition; the minus sign in the formula is there to make it so. Quick check: after dividing each substance's rate by its coefficient, all of them must agree.
Rates are measured by following anything that tracks one concentration: the color of a solution in a spectrometer, the pressure of a gas, the conductivity of ions or the volume of gas collected.

blocks.html: You know how to measure a rate. Experiments show that the rate depends on concentrations, and in a simple way: as a power of each concentration. That relationship is the rate law.

A rate law has the form $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^m[\mathrm{B}]^n$. The exponents $m$ and $n$ are the orders with respect to A and B, their sum is the overall order, and $k$ is the rate constant. Orders are found by experiment, not read from the balanced equation.

Why can't you read the orders from the coefficients? Most reactions do not happen in one collision. They run through a series of simpler steps, and the rate law reflects the slowest step and what comes before it, not the overall recipe. For example, $\mathrm{2N_2O_5 \to 4NO_2 + O_2}$ has the measured rate law $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]$: first order, not second. And for $\mathrm{NO_2 + CO \to NO + CO_2}$ below about $500\ \text{K}$, $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2$: carbon monoxide does not appear at all.

What each order means: with order 0, changing the concentration does nothing to the rate; with order 1, doubling it doubles the rate; with order 2, doubling it multiplies the rate by $2^2 = 4$. Orders are usually 0, 1 or 2, though fractions such as $\tfrac{1}{2}$ occur.

steps: Second order in NO, first order in $\mathrm{H_2}$, third order overall. Notice that $\mathrm{H_2}$ has coefficient 2 but order 1.
blocks.a: Orders 2 and 1 (overall 3), $k$ in $\text{M}^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, and the rate becomes 9 times larger.

blocks.title: Using a rate law

blocks.html: Writing the rate law from the balanced equation, as in $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]^2$ for $\mathrm{2N_2O_5 \to 4NO_2 + O_2}$. The coefficients describe the overall recipe, not the collisions that set the speed. Check: if a problem gives you only the balanced equation and no data or mechanism, you cannot know the orders.
The rate constant depends on temperature (and on a catalyst), but not on concentration. That is why one value of $k$ works for every experiment run at the same temperature.

A rate law has orders you must measure. The cleanest way is to run the reaction several times, change one starting concentration at a time, and measure the initial rate of each run. The math is solving an equation with the unknown in the exponent.

Pick two experiments in which only $[\mathrm{A}]$ changes. Then $\dfrac{\text{rate}_2}{\text{rate}_1} = \left(\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_2}{[\mathrm{A}]_1}\right)^m$, which gives the order $m$. Repeat for each reactant, then put any one experiment into the rate law to find $k$, with its units.

Divide the rate law for experiment 2 by the one for experiment 1. The rate constant cancels (same temperature), and every concentration that did not change cancels too. What remains links the rate ratio to the one concentration ratio. Initial rates are used because at the start nothing else has changed: no product has built up and no reactant has been used.

blocks.title: When the factor is not a whole number
blocks.q: When $[\mathrm{X}]$ goes from $0.40\ \text{M}$ to $0.60\ \text{M}$ (everything else fixed), the initial rate goes from $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$ to $7.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M/s}$. What is the order in X?

blocks.html: Comparing two experiments in which two concentrations changed at once. If $[\mathrm{A}]$ and $[\mathrm{B}]$ both doubled and the rate went up 8 times, you cannot tell which reactant caused how much of it. Look for a pair that differs in one concentration only. And always give $k$ with its units: a number alone does not say what the rate law is.

A first-order rate law, $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]$, says that the reactant disappears at a rate proportional to how much is left. That is the same rule as continuous exponential decay, so the concentration follows an exponential curve.

For a first-order reaction,
$$\ln[\mathrm{A}] = \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt \qquad\text{or}\qquad [\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0\,e^{-kt},$$
and the half-life $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$ is the same no matter how much reactant there is.

The rate law says $-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]$: the fraction that reacts in each small time interval is always the same, $k\,dt$. Separating and integrating, $\int \dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\int dt$ gives $\ln[\mathrm{A}] - \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 = -kt$. For the half-life, set $[\mathrm{A}] = \tfrac{1}{2}[\mathrm{A}]_0$: $\ln\tfrac{1}{2} = -kt_{1/2}$, so $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$. The starting amount cancels out, and that is why the half-life never changes.

blocks.title: Half-life and amount left
blocks.q: A first-order reaction has $k = 0.0200\ \text{min}^{-1}$ and $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.400\ \text{M}$. Find the half-life and $[\mathrm{A}]$ after $50.0\ \text{min}$.

blocks.title: How long to reach 10%
blocks.q: For the same reaction, how long until 10.0% of A is left?
steps: $$t = \dfrac{\ln 10.0}{0.0200\ \text{min}^{-1}} = \dfrac{2.303}{0.0200} = 115\ \text{min}$$ That is 3.32 half-lives, as it should be: $(\tfrac{1}{2})^{3.32} = 0.100$.

blocks.title: Fractions of a half-life
blocks.q: A reactant has a half-life of $12.0\ \text{min}$. What fraction is left after $30.0\ \text{min}$?
steps: Fraction left $= \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2.5} = 0.177$. This form is the same law: $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/t_{1/2}} = e^{-kt}$ because $k = \ln 2/t_{1/2}$.

blocks.html: Thinking the half-life gets longer (or shorter) as the reactant runs down. For first order the fraction that reacts per minute is fixed, so every half-life is the same length. Check: if a problem shows half-lives that change, the reaction is not first order.

Two measurements are enough to find $k$ for a first-order reaction: $k = \dfrac{1}{t_2 - t_1}\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_1}{[\mathrm{A}]_2}$. Because only the ratio of concentrations enters, you can use anything proportional to concentration, such as absorbance or the pressure of a gas, without converting it first. Many real processes behave this way: the decomposition of $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$, the loss of many drugs from the bloodstream, and every radioactive decay.
Radioactive decay is the most famous first-order process, which is why half-lives of isotopes are constants you can look up.

blocks.html: The first-order equations came from integrating $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]$. Integrating the zero- and second-order rate laws in the same way gives two more straight-line laws, each with its own half-life.

Zero order: $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$ and $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}$. Second order: $\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]} = \dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} + kt$ and $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{1}{k[\mathrm{A}]_0}$. Only the first-order half-life is independent of concentration.

Zero order: $-d[\mathrm{A}]/dt = k$ is a constant rate, so the concentration falls in a straight line. Second order: $-d[\mathrm{A}]/dt = k[\mathrm{A}]^2$; separating gives $\int [\mathrm{A}]^{-2}\,d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\int dt$, so $\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]} - \dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = kt$. Put $[\mathrm{A}] = \tfrac{1}{2}[\mathrm{A}]_0$ into each to get the half-lives. A second-order reaction slows sharply as A runs down (the rate goes as the square), so each half-life is twice as long as the one before. A zero-order reaction keeps its pace, so each half-life is half as long as the one before.

blocks.title: A second-order reaction
blocks.q: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2$ with $k = 0.50\ \text{M}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ and $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.20\ \text{M}$. Find the first half-life, the second half-life and $[\mathrm{A}]$ at $30\ \text{s}$.
steps: The second half-life starts at $0.10\ \text{M}$: $\dfrac{1}{(0.50)(0.10)} = 20\ \text{s}$, twice as long.

At $30\ \text{s}$: $$\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]} = \dfrac{1}{0.20} + (0.50)(30) = 5.0 + 15 = 20\ \text{M}^{-1}$$ so $[\mathrm{A}] = 0.050\ \text{M}$. That fits: 10 s plus 20 s is two half-lives, and $0.20 \to 0.10 \to 0.050$.

blocks.title: A zero-order reaction
blocks.q: A reaction on a catalyst surface is zero order with $k = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M/s}$ and $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.20\ \text{M}$. Find the half-life and when A runs out.
steps: $[\mathrm{A}] = 0$ when $0.20 = (5.0 \times 10^{-3})t$: $t = 40\ \text{s}$. The second "half-life" (from 0.10 M to 0.050 M) takes only 10 s.

blocks.html: Using $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$ for every reaction. That formula holds only for first order. Check the units of $k$: if $k$ is in $\text{M}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, the reaction is second order and its half-life needs $[\mathrm{A}]_0$.
Zero-order behavior is common when a reaction happens on a surface or on an enzyme that is fully occupied: adding more reactant cannot speed it up, because every site is already busy.

blocks.html: Each integrated rate law is a straight line in the right coordinates. So with one run of concentration against time, you can test all three orders at once. It is the same idea as fitting a linear model: the slope means something.

Plot $[\mathrm{A}]$, $\ln[\mathrm{A}]$ and $1/[\mathrm{A}]$ against time. The one that is straight tells the order (0, 1 or 2). Its slope gives $k$: slope $= -k$ for the first two plots and $+k$ for the $1/[\mathrm{A}]$ plot.

Each integrated law has the form $y = b + mx$ with time as $x$. Zero order: $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$. First order: $\ln[\mathrm{A}] = \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$. Second order: $1/[\mathrm{A}] = 1/[\mathrm{A}]_0 + kt$. Only the true order makes its plot a line; the other two curve.

blocks.html: Real data scatter a little, so no plot is perfectly straight. Fit a line to each of the three plots and keep the one whose points hug the line best (the correlation closest to $\pm 1$). Collect data over two or three half-lives: early on, all three plots look nearly straight, because any smooth curve does over a short stretch.

Choosing the plot that looks steepest, or the one that ends nearest zero. Steepness depends on the axis scale; what matters is whether the points lie on a line. And for zero and first order the slope is negative while $k$ is positive: $k = -\text{slope}$.

blocks.html: Reactions speed up when heated, often a lot. Activation energy explains why: only collisions with enough energy react, and heating raises the share of such collisions sharply. The Arrhenius equation turns that into a formula, and logarithms make it easy to use.

$k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$. Taking logs, $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}$, so a plot of $\ln k$ against $1/T$ is a line with slope $-E_a/R$. For two temperatures,
$$\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1} = -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$
with $T$ in kelvins and $E_a$ in J/mol when $R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$.

In a gas, the fraction of collisions with at least $E_a$ of energy is about $e^{-E_a/RT}$ (from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution). $A$ collects the rest: how often molecules collide and how often they meet in the right orientation. Because $T$ sits in an exponent, a small rise in temperature makes a large change in $k$. Subtract the logarithmic form at $T_1$ from the one at $T_2$ and $\ln A$ cancels, which gives the two-point form.

blocks.q: A rate constant doubles when the temperature rises from $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to $35\ ^\circ\text{C}$. What is $E_a$?
steps: This is the source of the old rule of thumb that a 10-degree rise doubles a rate near room temperature; it holds only for activation energies near 50 kJ/mol.

blocks.q: $E_a = 75.0\ \text{kJ/mol}$ and $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $300\ \text{K}$. Find $k$ at $320\ \text{K}$.

blocks.q: A plot of $\ln k$ against $1/T$ has slope $-6.00 \times 10^3\ \text{K}$. Find $E_a$.

blocks.html: Using Celsius temperatures, or putting $E_a$ in kJ/mol beside $R$ in J/(mol·K). Celsius gives wrong ratios (and division by zero at $0\ ^\circ\text{C}$), and mixed units make $E_a$ off by a factor of 1000. Check: $E_a/RT$ must be a pure number, typically between 10 and 40 for reactions you can watch.
Try it on the bench: in the Mixing Lab you can warm a reaction and add a catalyst, and watch how much faster it goes.

A rate law for an overall reaction must be measured. There is one exception: a reaction that happens in a single collision, an elementary step. For it, the rate law can be written straight from the equation.

The molecularity of an elementary step is the number of particles that collide in it: unimolecular (one), bimolecular (two) or termolecular (three, rare). For an elementary step only, the rate law uses the coefficients as orders: $\mathrm{A + B \to}$ products gives $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$, and $\mathrm{2A \to}$ products gives $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2$.

In a bimolecular step, every reaction event is a collision between one A and one B. The number of such collisions per second in a liter is proportional to $[\mathrm{A}]$ (more A to be hit) and to $[\mathrm{B}]$ (more B doing the hitting), so the rate is proportional to $[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$. For a unimolecular step, each molecule falls apart or rearranges on its own with a fixed chance per second, so the rate is $k[\mathrm{A}]$. Three particles rarely meet at the same instant, which is why termolecular steps are uncommon.

blocks.cap: A bimolecular step in a box of A and B. Add more A or more B: the reacting collisions per second go up in proportion to each, which is $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$.

blocks.title: A bimolecular step
blocks.q: The elementary step $\mathrm{NO + O_3 \to NO_2 + O_2}$ occurs in polluted air. Give its molecularity and rate law.
steps: Because it is elementary, the coefficients are the orders: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}][\mathrm{O_3}]$.

blocks.q: Write the rate law of the elementary step $\mathrm{2NO_2 \to NO_3 + NO}$.
steps: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2$: one factor for each colliding molecule.

blocks.html: Writing the rate law of an overall reaction from its coefficients as if it were one elementary step. $\mathrm{2N_2O_5 \to 4NO_2 + O_2}$ is not a collision of two molecules, and its measured rate law is first order. Check: the problem must say the step is elementary (or be part of a mechanism) before the coefficients become orders.
Molecularity is a whole number by its nature: you cannot have half a molecule colliding. Orders of overall reactions can be fractions, which is one sign that they come from several steps.
Most reactions are a sequence of elementary steps. The list of steps is the mechanism. A mechanism is a proposal: it must add up to the overall equation and agree with the measured rate law.

Add the steps and cancel what appears on both sides to get the overall equation. An intermediate is made in one step and used up in a later one. A catalyst is used up in one step and made again in a later one. Neither appears in the overall equation.

Think of an intermediate as a part that is built and then installed: it is a product first, a reactant later. A catalyst is a tool: it goes in at the start and comes back out at the end, ready to be used again. That order of appearance (product first or reactant first) is how you tell them apart in a list of steps.

blocks.title: Finding an intermediate
blocks.q:
A proposed mechanism for $\mathrm{NO_2 + CO \to NO + CO_2}$:
Step 1: $\mathrm{NO_2 + NO_2 \to NO_3 + NO}$
Step 2: $\mathrm{NO_3 + CO \to NO_2 + CO_2}$
Check that it adds up, and name any intermediate.
steps: Cancel $\mathrm{NO_3}$ (both sides) and one $\mathrm{NO_2}$: $\mathrm{NO_2 + CO \to NO + CO_2}$. It matches.
$\mathrm{NO_3}$ is made in step 1 and used in step 2: an intermediate.
blocks.a: It adds up; $\mathrm{NO_3}$ is the intermediate.

blocks.title: Telling a catalyst from an intermediate
blocks.q:
Chlorine atoms from CFCs destroy ozone in the stratosphere:
Step 1: $\mathrm{Cl + O_3 \to ClO + O_2}$
Step 2: $\mathrm{ClO + O \to Cl + O_2}$
Find the overall reaction, the catalyst and the intermediate.
steps: $\mathrm{Cl}$ is used in step 1 and made again in step 2: a catalyst. One chlorine atom can go around this cycle many thousands of times.
$\mathrm{ClO}$ is made in step 1 and used in step 2: an intermediate.
blocks.a: $\mathrm{O_3 + O \to 2O_2}$; Cl is the catalyst and ClO the intermediate.

blocks.name: ch-energydiagram
blocks.cap: An energy profile for a two-step mechanism. The intermediate sits in the valley between the two humps.

blocks.html: Mixing up intermediates and catalysts. Both cancel from the overall equation, but in opposite order. Check the first step in which the species appears: on the product side, it is an intermediate; on the reactant side (and it comes back later), it is a catalyst.

A mechanism can be ruled out by experiment, but never proven. Chemists test proposals by checking the rate law they predict, by detecting intermediates with spectroscopy, and by labeling atoms with isotopes to see where they end up. The next lessons show how a mechanism predicts a rate law.

items: The steps must add up to the overall equation.
Each step must be a plausible collision (one, two or rarely three particles).
The rate law it predicts must match the measured one.

blocks.html: A mechanism has several steps, usually running at very different speeds. The overall reaction cannot go faster than its slowest step, the way a line at a store moves only as fast as the slowest checkout.

The slowest step is the rate-determining step. When it is the first step, the rate law of the whole reaction is the rate law of that step: its reactants, raised to their coefficients. Fast steps after it do not appear in the rate law.

Products come out of the end of the mechanism only as fast as material passes through the slowest step. Steps after it are waiting for its product and finish almost at once, so changing their reactants' concentrations cannot speed anything up. Steps before it matter (the next lesson shows how), but when the slow step is first, nothing comes before it.

blocks.name: ch-energydiagram
blocks.cap: The first step has the higher barrier, so it is the slow step and sets the rate.

blocks.title: A slow first step
blocks.q:
Mechanism for $\mathrm{NO_2 + CO \to NO + CO_2}$:
Step 1 (slow): $\mathrm{2NO_2 \to NO_3 + NO}$
Step 2 (fast): $\mathrm{NO_3 + CO \to NO_2 + CO_2}$
What rate law does it predict?
steps: The slow step is the first step, and it is elementary: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2$.
CO reacts only in the fast step after it, so it does not appear: the reaction is zero order in CO.
This matches what is measured below about $500\ \text{K}$, which supports the mechanism.

blocks.title: A molecule falling apart first
blocks.q:
For $$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr} + \mathrm{OH^-} \to \mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH} + \mathrm{Br^-}$$:
Step 1 (slow): $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr \to (CH_3)_3C^+ + Br^-}$
Step 2 (fast): $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^+ + OH^- \to (CH_3)_3COH}$
Predict the rate law. Does doubling $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ change the rate?
steps: $\mathrm{OH^-}$ enters only after the slow step, so doubling it does not change the rate.

blocks.title: A mechanism that fails the test
blocks.q:
For $\mathrm{2A + B \to C}$ the measured rate law is $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2$. A student proposes:
Step 1 (slow): $\mathrm{A + B \to D}$
Step 2 (fast): $\mathrm{D + A \to C}$
Is this mechanism consistent with the data?
steps: The steps add up: $\mathrm{2A + B \to C}$, with D as an intermediate.
The slow first step predicts $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$: first order in B.
The measured law is second order in A and zero order in B. The prediction disagrees, so this mechanism is ruled out, even though it adds up correctly.
blocks.a: No: it predicts the wrong rate law.

blocks.html: Writing the rate law from a fast step, or including a species that reacts only after the slow step. Check: every species in your rate law must take part in the slow step or in a step before it. If the slow step is not the first step, you will need the method in the next lesson.
"Slow" here means slow compared with the other steps. A rate-determining step can still finish in a fraction of a second.

When the slow step comes second, its rate law usually contains an intermediate. Intermediates are hard to measure and do not appear in a measured rate law, so we need a way to replace them. The trick uses dynamic equilibrium.

If a fast, reversible first step comes before the slow step, its forward and reverse rates are equal: $k_1[\text{reactants}] = k_{-1}[\text{intermediate}]$. Solve for the intermediate and substitute into the slow step's rate law. The final rate law contains only reactants (and sometimes products).

The first step goes back and forth many times while the slow step barely runs. So it has time to settle into equilibrium, and only a trickle of intermediate leaks away through the slow step. Setting the two rates equal is the same as writing the equilibrium constant of the first step, $K_1 = k_1/k_{-1}$.

blocks.title: Nitrogen monoxide and oxygen
blocks.q:
Mechanism for $\mathrm{2NO + O_2 \to 2NO_2}$:
Step 1 (fast, reversible): $\mathrm{2NO \rightleftharpoons N_2O_2}$
Step 2 (slow): $\mathrm{N_2O_2 + O_2 \to 2NO_2}$
Derive the rate law.
steps: Slow step: $\text{rate} = k_2[\mathrm{N_2O_2}][\mathrm{O_2}]$. $\mathrm{N_2O_2}$ is an intermediate, so it must go.

blocks.title: Hydrogen and iodine
blocks.q:
A mechanism for $\mathrm{H_2 + I_2 \to 2HI}$:
Step 1 (fast, reversible): $\mathrm{I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2I}$
Step 2 (slow): $\mathrm{H_2 + 2I \to 2HI}$
Derive the rate law.
steps: $\text{rate} = \dfrac{k_2k_1}{k_{-1}}[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]$. Notice: this rate law looks just like one elementary collision of $\mathrm{H_2}$ with $\mathrm{I_2}$, yet the mechanism is different. A rate law alone cannot prove a mechanism.

blocks.name: ch-energydiagram
blocks.cap: A low first barrier lets step 1 run back and forth quickly and settle into equilibrium; the high second barrier is the slow step.

blocks.html: Leaving the intermediate's concentration in the final rate law. A measured rate law contains only species you can add to the flask. Check: after substituting, scan the rate law for anything that is made in one step and used in another; if you find it, substitute again.
An overall order of 3 (as in the NO example) is one hint of a pre-equilibrium: three-body collisions are rare, but a fast equilibrium followed by a two-body collision gives the same rate law.
For one step, an energy profile has one hump, the activation energy. For a mechanism with several steps, the profile has one hump per step, with valleys between them.

Each peak is a transition state: a fleeting arrangement at the top of a barrier that cannot be isolated. Each valley between peaks is an intermediate: a real species that lasts long enough, at least in principle, to be detected. The step with the tallest climb (measured from the valley just before it) is usually the slow step.

A transition state is the point of highest energy along one step, with bonds half made and half broken; molecules pass through it in about a trillionth of a second. An intermediate sits in a dip: it has to climb over a barrier to go anywhere, so it survives for a while. The rate of each step depends on the height of its own barrier, so the highest climb is the bottleneck. The overall $\Delta H$ is simply the energy of the products minus that of the reactants, no matter how many steps lie between.

blocks.name: ch-energydiagram
blocks.cap: The second example's profile: reactants at 0, the first peak at 80, an intermediate at 30, the second peak at 70 and products at −40 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: Reading a profile
blocks.q: An energy profile has three peaks and ends lower than it starts. How many steps does the mechanism have, how many intermediates, and is the reaction exothermic?
steps: One peak per step: three steps.
The valleys between peaks are intermediates: two of them.

blocks.title: Finding the slow step
blocks.q: Energies along a two-step profile (kJ/mol): reactants 0, first transition state 80, intermediate 30, second transition state 70, products −40. Which step is slow? What is $\Delta H$?
steps: Step 2: climb from the intermediate at 30 to 70, so $E_{a2} = 40\ \text{kJ/mol}$.
Step 1 has the larger barrier: it is the slow step. $\Delta H = -40 - 0 = -40\ \text{kJ/mol}$.

blocks.html: Picking the step with the biggest drop in energy as the slow step, or calling a peak an intermediate. How far a step falls says how much energy it releases, not how fast it goes; speed is set by the climb. Check: intermediates are in valleys, transition states are on peaks.

Strictly, what controls the overall rate is how high the highest transition state lies above the starting point. In the simple profiles of this course, that is the step with the tallest climb from the valley before it.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up. With multistep energy profiles we can say exactly how: it provides a different mechanism, whose highest barrier is lower.

A catalyst opens a new pathway with a lower activation energy. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so it does not change $K$, $\Delta H$ or the amount of product at equilibrium; it only gets there sooner. Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as the reactants, heterogeneous ones are in a different phase (usually a solid surface), and enzymes are biological catalysts.

Forward and reverse reactions pass over the same peak, in opposite directions. Lower the peak and both directions speed up equally. Because $K = k_\text{f}/k_\text{r}$, the ratio stays the same. Since the rate constant depends on $e^{-E_a/RT}$, even a modest drop in $E_a$ gives a big factor in rate.

blocks.name: ch-energydiagram
blocks.cap: Toggle the catalyst. The barrier drops for both directions, but the start and end energies (and so $\Delta H$) stay put.

blocks.name: ch-collisions
blocks.cap: With the catalyst on, a larger share of the same collisions has enough energy to react.

blocks.title: A homogeneous catalyst
blocks.q:
Iodide ion speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide:
Step 1 (slow): $\mathrm{H_2O_2 + I^- \to H_2O + IO^-}$
Step 2 (fast): $\mathrm{H_2O_2 + IO^- \to H_2O + O_2 + I^-}$
Find the overall reaction, the catalyst and the intermediate.
steps: $\mathrm{I^-}$ is used in step 1 and remade in step 2: the catalyst. It is in solution with the peroxide, so it is homogeneous.
$\mathrm{IO^-}$ is made and then used: the intermediate.

blocks.title: How much faster?
blocks.q: A catalyst lowers $E_a$ by $20.0\ \text{kJ/mol}$ at $298\ \text{K}$. If $A$ is unchanged, by what factor does $k$ grow?

items: Heterogeneous: the platinum, palladium and rhodium in a car's catalytic converter turn CO and NO into $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$ on their surfaces; iron catalyzes the Haber process for ammonia.
Enzymes: catalase, in nearly every cell, breaks down hydrogen peroxide millions of times per second per enzyme molecule.

blocks.html: Thinking a catalyst raises the yield at equilibrium, or that it speeds up only the forward reaction. It lowers the barrier for both directions, so equilibrium comes sooner but lies in the same place. Check: a catalyst never appears in $K$ and never changes $\Delta H$.

At dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate and the concentrations stop changing. Experiments show something striking: whatever amounts you start with, one particular combination of the equilibrium concentrations always comes out the same at a given temperature. That number is the equilibrium constant.

For $a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}$,
$$K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}$$
using equilibrium concentrations: products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient. Pure solids and pure liquids are left out. $K$ depends only on temperature.

For one elementary step, $\mathrm{A + B \rightleftharpoons C}$, equilibrium means $k_\text{f}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}] = k_\text{r}[\mathrm{C}]$, so $\dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]} = \dfrac{k_\text{f}}{k_\text{r}}$, a constant. Thermodynamics shows the same form holds for any balanced equation, whatever the mechanism. Solids and pure liquids drop out because $K$ really uses activities: concentration relative to $1\ \text{M}$ for solutes, pressure relative to $1\ \text{bar}$ for gases, and exactly 1 for a pure solid or liquid, whose "concentration" cannot change. That is also why $K$ has no units.

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: Nitrogen and hydrogen approaching equilibrium. Q climbs until it equals K, and then the concentrations hold steady.

blocks.title: Writing K
blocks.q: Write $K_c$ for $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}$ and for $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)}$.
steps: Ammonia: products over reactants, with the coefficients as powers: $K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2}][\mathrm{H_2}]^3}$.
Limestone: both solids are left out, so $K_c = [\mathrm{CO_2}]$. At a given temperature the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ concentration over the solids is fixed, however much solid is there.

blocks.title: A value from data
blocks.q: At $703\ \text{K}$, an equilibrium mixture of $\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}$ has $[\mathrm{H_2}] = [\mathrm{I_2}] = 0.0100\ \text{M}$ and $[\mathrm{HI}] = 0.0737\ \text{M}$. Find $K_c$.

blocks.html: In water, the solvent is a pure liquid too, so $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ is left out of expressions such as $K_a$. But water vapor, $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$, is a gas and stays in.

A value of $K$ belongs to one balanced equation at one temperature. Write the equation differently and $K$ changes (see manipulating K); change the temperature and $K$ changes too. For gases, $K$ can also be written with partial pressures, as Kp.

Putting solids or pure liquids into $K$, or forgetting the powers. $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}$ does not belong in its own decomposition constant, and $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ must be cubed in the ammonia expression. Check: every term in $K$ is an (aq) or (g) species, with its coefficient as the exponent.
An equilibrium constant is products over reactants. So its size tells you, at a glance, which side wins.

When $K$ is large (roughly above $10^3$), the equilibrium mixture is mostly products. When $K$ is small (below about $10^{-3}$), it is mostly reactants. Near 1, both are present in similar amounts. $K$ says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

If $K = [\mathrm{B}]/[\mathrm{A}] = 1000$ for $\mathrm{A \rightleftharpoons B}$, there are a thousand B for every A at equilibrium: the reaction has gone essentially to completion. If $K = 10^{-3}$, the ratio is reversed. Speed is a different question, set by the activation energy: $K$ compares the end states, not the barrier between them.

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: A reaction with K = 100 (the forward rate constant 100 times the reverse). At equilibrium, B outnumbers A about 100 to 1.

blocks.title: How much product?
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{A \rightleftharpoons B}$, $K = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$. At equilibrium $[\mathrm{A}] = 0.50\ \text{M}$. What is $[\mathrm{B}]$?
steps: $[\mathrm{B}] = 5.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{M}$: almost all of it is still A.

blocks.title: Large K, no reaction
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2H_2O(g)}$ at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $K$ is about $10^{80}$. Yet a balloon of hydrogen and oxygen can sit for years unchanged. Why?
steps: The huge $K$ means that at equilibrium essentially all of it would be water.
But the reaction has a high activation energy, so at room temperature it goes immeasurably slowly. A spark supplies the energy, and then it is explosive.
blocks.a: $K$ describes where the reaction ends, not how fast it gets there.

At equilibrium
Example

blocks.html: Thinking a large $K$ means a fast reaction. $K$ compares products with reactants at the end; the rate depends on the activation energy. Check: the speed of a reaction is never computed from $K$.

When $K$ is between about $10^{-3}$ and $10^{3}$, you cannot guess the mixture by eye: it takes an ICE-table calculation. Remember too that $K$ changes with temperature, so "mostly products" at one temperature can become "mostly reactants" at another.
The tiny $K$ for nitrogen and oxygen is lucky for us: air would otherwise turn into nitrogen oxides. In hot car engines and lightning, $K$ is much larger, and some NO forms.

Equilibrium constants are tabulated for particular equations. Often you need $K$ for the same reaction written differently, or for a combination of reactions. Because $K$ is built from the equilibrium expression, you can work it out from what happens to that expression.
Reverse the equation: $K' = 1/K$. Multiply every coefficient by $n$: $K' = K^n$ (so halving gives $\sqrt{K}$). Add two equations: $K = K_1 \times K_2$.

Reversing swaps the top and bottom of the expression, so it becomes the reciprocal. Doubling every coefficient doubles every exponent, which squares the whole fraction. When you add two equations, multiplying their expressions makes the concentrations of species that cancel (appearing in the top of one and the bottom of the other) cancel in the product too, leaving the expression for the sum.

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: Starting from B alone, the same equilibrium is reached as from A. Read backward, the same mixture gives $[\mathrm{A}]/[\mathrm{B}] = 1/K$.

blocks.title: Reverse and scale
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}$, $K = 0.50$ at $673\ \text{K}$. Find $K$ for $\mathrm{2NH_3 \rightleftharpoons N_2 + 3H_2}$ and for $\mathrm{\tfrac{1}{2}N_2 + \tfrac{3}{2}H_2 \rightleftharpoons NH_3}$.

blocks.title: Adding reactions
blocks.q: At some temperature, $\mathrm{A \rightleftharpoons B}$ has $K_1 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ and $\mathrm{B \rightleftharpoons 2C}$ has $K_2 = 4.0 \times 10^{2}$. Find $K$ for $\mathrm{A \rightleftharpoons 2C}$.

blocks.title: Reverse one, then add
blocks.q: $\mathrm{X \rightleftharpoons Y}$ has $K_1 = 5.0$, and $\mathrm{Z \rightleftharpoons Y}$ has $K_2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}$. Find $K$ for $\mathrm{X \rightleftharpoons Z}$.
steps: To get Z on the right, reverse the second: $\mathrm{Y \rightleftharpoons Z}$, $K = 1/(2.0 \times 10^{-2}) = 50$.

blocks.html: These rules are how chemists find constants that are hard to measure directly. If two reactions with known $K$ add up to the one you care about, multiply their constants. The same idea, in the language of energy, is Hess's law: free energies add when equations add, and since $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$, adding $\Delta G^\circ$ values means multiplying $K$ values.

Doubling $K$ when the equation is doubled, or adding $K$ values when the reactions are added. The changes act on exponents and on a fraction, so they become powers and products. Check: a reaction and its reverse must have $K \times K' = 1$.
This rule is the reason Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate acid–base pair, and why coupled reactions multiply their constants.

For gases you can write $K$ with partial pressures instead of concentrations. The ideal gas law connects the two: $P = \dfrac{n}{V}RT$, and $\dfrac{n}{V}$ is the molar concentration. So each pressure is a concentration times $RT$.
$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ = (moles of gas on the product side) − (moles of gas on the reactant side), $R = 0.08206\ \text{L·atm/(mol·K)}$ and $T$ is in kelvins.

Replace each pressure in $K_p$ with $[\mathrm{X}]RT$. Every product term brings a factor $RT$ to its coefficient's power on top, and every reactant term the same on the bottom. All the concentration factors together make $K_c$; the leftover factors of $RT$ give $(RT)^{c+d-a-b} = (RT)^{\Delta n}$. Solids and liquids have no partial pressure, so they do not count in $\Delta n$. The value of $R$ must match the units: pressures in atm and concentrations in mol/L call for $0.08206\ \text{L·atm/(mol·K)}$.

blocks.name: ch-gasbox
blocks.cap: Each gas has its own partial pressure, set by its amount per liter and the temperature: $P = (n/V)RT$.

blocks.title: Fewer moles of gas
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}$, $K_c = 0.50$ at $673\ \text{K}$. Find $K_p$.

blocks.title: More moles of gas
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{PCl_5(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g)}$, $K_c = 0.042$ at $523\ \text{K}$. Find $K_p$.

blocks.title: A solid in the equation
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{C(s) + CO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2CO(g)}$, what is $\Delta n$, and when would $K_p = K_c$?
steps: Count gases only: $\Delta n = 2 - 1 = +1$. Carbon, a solid, does not count.
$K_p = K_c$ only when $\Delta n = 0$, as in $\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}$; then $(RT)^0 = 1$.

blocks.title: Going back to Kc
blocks.q: At $673\ \text{K}$, $K_p = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ for $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}$. Recover $K_c$.
steps: Solve the relation for $K_c$: $K_c = K_p(RT)^{-\Delta n} = K_p(RT)^{2}$.
$$K_c = (1.6 \times 10^{-4})(55.2)^2 = (1.6 \times 10^{-4})(3.05 \times 10^{3}) = 0.49$$ matching the 0.50 we started from (the small gap is rounding).

blocks.html: Strictly, both constants are written with activities, so both are pure numbers: pressures are divided by the standard pressure and concentrations by $1\ \text{M}$. That is why we report $K_p$ and $K_c$ without units, even though the conversion factor $(RT)^{\Delta n}$ looks as if it carries some.

Counting solids and liquids in $\Delta n$, or using $R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$. Only gases have partial pressures, and $8.314$ belongs with energies, not with atm and liters. Check: if $\Delta n$ is negative, $K_p$ should be smaller than $K_c$ at ordinary temperatures (where $RT > 1$).

The equilibrium expression can be evaluated for any mixture, not only one at equilibrium. The result is called the reaction quotient, $Q$. Comparing it with $K$ tells you which way the reaction will go.

$Q$ has the same form as $K$ but uses the current concentrations. If $Q < K$, the reaction goes forward (toward products). If $Q > K$, it goes in reverse (toward reactants). If $Q = K$, it is at equilibrium.

A reaction always moves toward equilibrium, where $Q = K$. If $Q$ is too small, there is too little product compared with reactant; making more product raises the top of the fraction and lowers the bottom, so $Q$ climbs to $K$. If $Q$ is too big, the reverse reaction brings it down.

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: Partway through, extra $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ is added. Q jumps above K, and the reaction runs in reverse until Q falls back to K.

blocks.title: Q below K
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)}$, $K_c = 4.6 \times 10^{-3}$ at $298\ \text{K}$. A flask holds $0.10\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ and $0.010\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{NO_2}$. Which way does it go?
steps: $Q < K$: there is too little $\mathrm{NO_2}$. The reaction goes forward, making more $\mathrm{NO_2}$.

blocks.title: Q above K
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}$, $K_c = 54.3$ at $703\ \text{K}$. A mixture has $[\mathrm{HI}] = 0.50\ \text{M}$ and $[\mathrm{H_2}] = [\mathrm{I_2}] = 0.050\ \text{M}$. Which way does it go?
steps: $Q > K$: too much HI. The reverse reaction runs, turning some HI into $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{I_2}$.

blocks.title: A solid in the mixture
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)}$ at a certain temperature, $K_p = 0.25$. A sealed flask holds both solids and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ at $0.40\ \text{atm}$. Which way does it go?
steps: Solids are left out, so $Q = P_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.40$.
$Q > K_p$: too much $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Some of it reacts with CaO to re-form $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ until the pressure falls to 0.25 atm.

blocks.html: Saying a reaction with $Q < K$ shifts toward reactants. It is the other way: small $Q$ means not enough products yet. Check with the extreme case: a flask with only reactants has $Q = 0$, and it obviously reacts forward.
$Q$ is also the bridge to free energy: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q is negative exactly when $Q < K$.

To find $K$ you need every equilibrium concentration, but experiments usually measure only one. The coefficients of the balanced equation link the others to it, using the same mole ratios as in stoichiometry. An ICE table keeps track.

Make a table with three rows: Initial, Change and Equilibrium. Put the known change for one species in the C row, scale it by the coefficients for every other species (minus for reactants, plus for products), add down the columns, and put the E row into $K$.

The amounts react in the ratio of the coefficients, just as they do in a reaction that goes to completion. The only difference is that the reaction stops at equilibrium instead of when a reactant runs out. Concentrations in one container change in the same ratio as moles, so the C row is just a mole ratio.

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: The ICE table updates as the mixture reacts. The changes for $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{NH_3}$ are always in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2.

blocks.title: One measured amount
blocks.q: A flask starts with $0.400\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $0.200\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{O_2}$. At equilibrium, $[\mathrm{SO_3}] = 0.300\ \text{M}$ in $\mathrm{2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)}$. Find $K_c$.
steps: I: $\mathrm{SO_2}$ 0.400, $\mathrm{O_2}$ 0.200, $\mathrm{SO_3}$ 0. C: $\mathrm{SO_3}$ $+0.300$, so $\mathrm{SO_2}$ $-0.300$ (same coefficient) and $\mathrm{O_2}$ $-0.150$ (half as much).

blocks.title: Equal starting amounts
blocks.q: $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{I_2}$, each $1.00\ \text{M}$, react in a sealed flask: $\mathrm{H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI}$. At equilibrium $[\mathrm{HI}] = 1.57\ \text{M}$. Find $K_c$.
steps: HI rose by 1.57, so $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{I_2}$ each fell by half of that: $0.785\ \text{M}$.

blocks.html: Two habits prevent most errors. First, work in molarities: if you are given moles and a volume, divide before you fill in the table (for a reaction in one container, moles also work in the C row, but $K_c$ needs molarities). Second, make the C row from a single unknown and the coefficients, then check that the E row has no negative entries.

Putting the starting concentrations into $K$, or using the same change for every species. $K$ needs equilibrium values, and the changes follow the coefficients: when 2 $\mathrm{SO_3}$ form, only 1 $\mathrm{O_2}$ is used. Check: the C row should be proportional to the coefficients, with opposite signs on the two sides.

Now run the ICE table the other way: you know $K$ and the starting amounts, and you want the equilibrium amounts. First use Q to see which way the reaction goes, call the unknown change $x$, and solve. Often that means the quadratic formula.

Write the E row in terms of $x$, substitute into the expression for $K$, and solve for $x$. Keep only the root that makes every concentration positive (and no larger than what you started with). Then check by putting the answers back into $K$.

A quadratic has two roots, but only one describes a real mixture. The other one would use up more reactant than the flask holds, or give a negative concentration. The algebra cannot know that; you can.

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: Starting with $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ only, some of it splits into $\mathrm{NO_2}$ until Q reaches K. The equilibrium row of the table comes from solving the equation for $x$.

blocks.title: A perfect square
blocks.q: $\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}$, $K_c = 54.3$. Starting with $0.200\ \text{M}$ each of $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{I_2}$ and no HI, find the equilibrium concentrations.
steps: $Q = 0 < K$, so the reaction goes forward. E row: $[\mathrm{H_2}] = [\mathrm{I_2}] = 0.200 - x$, $[\mathrm{HI}] = 2x$.
$54.3 = \dfrac{(2x)^2}{(0.200 - x)^2}$. Both sides are squares, so take the square root: $7.37 = \dfrac{2x}{0.200 - x}$.

blocks.title: Using the quadratic formula
blocks.q: $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)}$, $K_c = 4.6 \times 10^{-3}$. A flask starts with $0.100\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$. Find the equilibrium concentrations.
steps: Quadratic formula with $a = 4$, $b = 4.6 \times 10^{-3}$, $c = -4.6 \times 10^{-4}$: $b^2 - 4ac = 7.38 \times 10^{-3}$, whose square root is $0.0859$.
The roots are $0.0102$ and $-0.0113$. The negative root would make $[\mathrm{NO_2}]$ negative, so $x = 0.0102$.

blocks.html: Keeping the root that makes a concentration negative, or larger than the amount you started with. Check every concentration in the E row after you pick $x$, and confirm that they reproduce $K$.
If the reaction goes in reverse ($Q > K$), write the change with the opposite signs: reactants $+x$, products $-$(coefficient)$x$.
Solving for equilibrium concentrations often leads to a quadratic or worse. When $K$ is very small, a shortcut avoids it: so little reacts that $x$ hardly changes the starting amount.

If $K$ is small compared with the starting concentration, replace $C - x$ by $C$, solve the simpler equation, and then check: if $x$ is less than 5% of $C$, the answer is good. If not, go back and solve exactly.

Subtracting a small number from a large one barely changes it: $0.10 - 0.0003 = 0.0997$, within 0.3% of 0.10. Dropping $x$ there changes the answer by about the same small fraction, which is less than the uncertainty in most values of $K$. The 5% rule is a common agreed limit for "small enough." The approximation is only for $x$ beside a larger number; $x$ standing alone, as in $x^2$, must stay.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: The exact expression $x^2/(C - x)$ and the approximation $x^2/C$. For small $x$ the curves overlap; as $x$ becomes a sizable part of $C$ they pull apart. Slide $C$ down to see the trouble start sooner.

blocks.title: The approximation works
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{A \rightleftharpoons B + C}$, $K = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$, and $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.10\ \text{M}$. Find $x = [\mathrm{B}]$ at equilibrium.
steps: Check: $\dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-4}}{0.10} = 0.32\%$, well under 5%. The approximation holds.

blocks.html: A quick test before you start: if $C/K$ is larger than about 400, the 5% rule will usually pass for a reaction like these. The check afterward is still the rule.

You will use this approximation constantly in weak-acid and weak-base problems, where $K_a$ or $K_b$ is usually small and the 5% check usually passes. When it fails, the quadratic formula is always there, and a calculator's equation solver gives the same root in seconds; the approximation's real value is that it shows how the answer depends on $K$ and $C$.

Dropping $x$ when $K$ is large, or never checking whether the approximation held. A large $K$ means most of the reactant reacts, so $x$ is not small at all. Check: always divide $x$ by the starting amount and compare with 5%.

Le Chatelier’s principle says an equilibrium shifts to undo a disturbance. With Q and K you can see why, and predict the direction every time: a disturbance either changes $Q$ (and the reaction runs until $Q = K$ again) or changes $K$ itself.

Adding or removing a species, or changing the volume, changes $Q$ but not $K$. The reaction then runs in the direction that brings $Q$ back to $K$. Only a change in temperature changes $K$. Adding an inert gas at constant volume changes nothing. A catalyst changes nothing either.

Halving the volume doubles every gas concentration. Each concentration in $Q$ is raised to its coefficient, so $Q$ is multiplied by $2^{\Delta n}$. For $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}$, $\Delta n = -2$, so $Q$ drops to $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of $K$ and the reaction moves forward, toward fewer moles of gas. An inert gas raises the total pressure but leaves each reacting gas's concentration (and partial pressure) unchanged, so $Q$ stays equal to $K$. Temperature is different: $K$ itself depends on it. For an exothermic reaction, $K$ gets smaller as $T$ rises.

blocks.html: You met pH and pOH as a scale from 0 to 14. Here we compute them exactly with logarithms, starting with strong acids and bases, which ionize completely.

$\text{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, $\text{pOH} = -\log[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, and at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$, so $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14.00$. A strong acid gives $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ equal to its concentration; a strong base gives $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ equal to its concentration times the number of $\mathrm{OH^-}$ per formula unit.

Water ionizes slightly: $\mathrm{2H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + OH^-}$, with $K_w = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}]$. Taking $-\log$ of both sides turns the product into a sum: $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = \text{p}K_w = 14.00$. The strong acids ($\mathrm{HCl}$, $\mathrm{HBr}$, $\mathrm{HI}$, $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, $\mathrm{HClO_4}$ and the first proton of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$) give up their protons completely, so no equilibrium calculation is needed. The strong bases are the Group 1 hydroxides and $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$, $\mathrm{Sr(OH)_2}$ and $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$, which release two $\mathrm{OH^-}$ each.

blocks.html: A weak acid ionizes only partly, so it reaches an equilibrium with water. Its equilibrium constant measures its strength. This builds on Brønsted–Lowry pairs and on pH.

For $\mathrm{HA + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + A^-}$, $K_a = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$, and $\text{p}K_a = -\log K_a$. A larger $K_a$ (smaller $\text{p}K_a$) means a stronger acid. For a base, $K_b = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HB^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}]}{[\mathrm{B}]}$. For any conjugate pair, $K_a \times K_b = K_w$, so $\text{p}K_a + \text{p}K_b = 14.00$ at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

Add the acid's ionization to its conjugate base's reaction with water:
$\mathrm{HA + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + A^-}$ ($K_a$)
$\mathrm{A^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HA + OH^-}$ ($K_b$)
The sum is $\mathrm{2H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + OH^-}$, whose constant is $K_w$. Adding reactions multiplies their constants, so $K_aK_b = K_w$. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base, and the product is always fixed.

The difference is $9.31 - 3.17 = 6.14$ units, so HF's $K_a$ is $10^{6.14} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{6}$ times larger.
blocks.a: HF, by a factor of about a million.

blocks.html: Strong acids have $K_a$ values far above 1, so large that they are hard to measure; in water they all look equally strong, because each one gives its proton to water completely. Weak acids have $K_a$ below 1, and their $\text{p}K_a$ values usually lie between about 2 and 12, a span of ten powers of ten in strength.

Thinking a larger $\text{p}K_a$ means a stronger acid. The "p" means minus the log, so large $\text{p}K_a$ means small $K_a$: a weak acid. Check: strong-ish weak acids such as HF have $\text{p}K_a$ near 3; very weak ones such as HCN are near 9.
Values of $K_a$ and $K_b$ in these lessons are at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ from the tables in the back of OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

blocks.html: For a weak acid, $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ is not the acid's concentration; only a small part ionizes. Its Ka and an ICE table give the answer, and the small-x approximation usually makes it quick.
For a weak acid at concentration $C$: $K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{C - x}$ with $x = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$. If $x$ is under 5% of $C$, then $x \approx \sqrt{K_aC}$. Then $\text{pH} = -\log x$.

Each HA that ionizes makes one $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ and one $\mathrm{A^-}$, so both equal $x$, and $C - x$ acid is left. The water's own $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ ($10^{-7}\ \text{M}$ at most) is tiny next to $x$ in any ordinary weak acid solution, so it is ignored. Because $K_a$ is small, $x$ is usually much smaller than $C$, which lets you drop it from $C - x$.

blocks.html: The weak-acid calculation gives $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$. Dividing by the starting concentration tells you what share of the acid molecules ionized, and that share depends on how dilute the solution is.

$\text{percent ionization} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]_\text{eq}}{C} \times 100\%$. When the small-x approximation holds, it is about $\sqrt{K_a/C} \times 100\%$, so diluting a weak acid makes a larger fraction of it ionize (even though $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ goes down).

Ionization makes two particles from one: $\mathrm{HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-}$ (water left out). Dilute an equilibrium mixture tenfold: the top of $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$ falls by $10 \times 10 = 100$ and the bottom by 10, so $Q$ drops to $\tfrac{1}{10}K$. The reaction shifts forward, ionizing more. Algebraically, $x/C \approx \sqrt{K_aC}/C = \sqrt{K_a/C}$: a hundredfold dilution gives ten times the percent ionization.

blocks.html: A weak base takes a proton from water and leaves $\mathrm{OH^-}$ behind. The calculation is the weak-acid one with $K_b$ in place of $K_a$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ in place of $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$, plus one last step from pOH to pH.

For $\mathrm{B + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HB^+ + OH^-}$: $K_b = \dfrac{x^2}{C - x}$ with $x = [\mathrm{OH^-}]$; often $x \approx \sqrt{K_bC}$. Then $\text{pOH} = -\log x$ and $\text{pH} = 14.00 - \text{pOH}$.

Ammonia and the amines have a lone pair on nitrogen that can accept a proton from water. Each base molecule that does so makes one $\mathrm{HB^+}$ and one $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so the ICE table is the same as for a weak acid. The equation gives $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, not $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, so you get the pOH first.

blocks.html: A salt is made of ions, and some ions are weak acids or weak bases. Using Ka × Kb = Kw and the weak-base method, you can predict and compute the pH of a salt solution.

Ions from strong acids and strong bases ($\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$) do not change the pH. The conjugate base of a weak acid ($\mathrm{F^-}$, $\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}$, $\mathrm{CN^-}$) makes the solution basic. The conjugate acid of a weak base ($\mathrm{NH_4^+}$) makes it acidic, and so do small, highly charged metal ions such as $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$.

$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is the conjugate base of HCl, a strong acid, so its $K_b$ is essentially zero: it does not take protons from water. $\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}$ is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so its $K_b = K_w/K_a$ is small but real, and it makes a little $\mathrm{OH^-}$. A metal ion such as $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ is surrounded by water molecules; its strong positive charge pulls on their O–H bonds, and one of those waters can release a proton: $$\mathrm{[Al(H_2O)_6]^{3+}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{[Al(H_2O)_5(OH)]^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_3O^+}$$

blocks.html: Some acids can give up more than one proton: carbonic acid ($\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$), sulfurous acid, phosphoric acid ($\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$), and vitamin C. Each proton comes off in its own step, each a weak-acid equilibrium with its own $K_a$.

The constants fall steeply: $K_{a1} \gg K_{a2} \gg K_{a3}$, usually by a factor of $10^4$ or more. So the pH comes almost entirely from the first step, treated as a single weak acid. In a solution of the acid alone, the concentration of the ion made in the second step, $[\mathrm{A^{2-}}]$, is about equal to $K_{a2}$.

Taking a proton from a neutral molecule is easier than taking one from an anion that already has a negative charge, and harder still from a 2− ion: the leftover charge holds the next proton back. Also, the $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ from step 1 pushes step 2 backward (a common-ion effect). In $K_{a2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{HA^-}]}$, step 1 makes $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}] \approx [\mathrm{HA^-}]$, so they cancel and $[\mathrm{A^{2-}}] \approx K_{a2}$.

Sulfuric acid is the exception you meet most: its first proton is strong. Its second, $K_{a2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}$, is weak but large enough that it must be solved as its own equilibrium in dilute solutions.

Why is HCl strong and HF weak? Why is $\mathrm{HClO_4}$ strong and HClO weak? The answers come from the bond to the acidic hydrogen and from how well the conjugate base holds its negative charge. You will use electronegativity, bond strength and resonance, and compare acids by Ka.

An acid is stronger when the H–A bond is weaker (easier to break) and more polar, and when the anion left behind spreads or stabilizes its negative charge. Down a group, bond strength wins: $\mathrm{HF \ll HCl < HBr < HI}$. Across a period, polarity wins: $\mathrm{CH_4 < NH_3 < H_2O < HF}$. For oxyacids, more O atoms and a more electronegative central atom make a stronger acid.

Binary acids: going down Group 17 the halogen grows, the H–X bond gets longer and much weaker (H–F 565, H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ/mol), and the proton leaves more easily. Across a period the atoms are similar in size, so the deciding factor is electronegativity: a more electronegative atom polarizes the bond and holds the negative charge better. Oxyacids all lose a proton from an O–H group. Extra O atoms on the central atom pull electron density away from that O–H bond, and in the anion they share the negative charge by resonance, which steadies it.

blocks.name: ch-lewis
blocks.cap: Acetate's two resonance forms: the negative charge is shared by both O atoms. Ethoxide, from ethanol, has no such sharing, which is why acetic acid is about $10^{11}$ times stronger than ethanol.

blocks.title: The chlorine oxyacids
blocks.q: Rank HClO, $\mathrm{HClO_2}$, $\mathrm{HClO_3}$ and $\mathrm{HClO_4}$ by strength, and explain.
steps: They differ only in the number of O atoms on Cl: 0, 1, 2 and 3 besides the OH.

Each extra O pulls electron density from the O–H bond and gives the anion one more atom to share the charge. Measured: HClO $K_a = 2.9 \times 10^{-8}$, $\mathrm{HClO_2}$ $1.1 \times 10^{-2}$, and $\mathrm{HClO_3}$ and $\mathrm{HClO_4}$ are strong.

blocks.title: Same shape, different halogen
blocks.q: Which is the stronger acid, HOCl or HOI?
steps: Both have one O–H with the halogen on the O. Chlorine is more electronegative than iodine.
Cl pulls more electron density through the O, weakening the O–H bond and steadying $\mathrm{ClO^-}$. HOCl: $K_a = 2.9 \times 10^{-8}$; HOI: $2.3 \times 10^{-11}$.

blocks.q: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ has $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ and $\mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}$ has $K_a = 1.4 \times 10^{-3}$. Explain the difference.
steps: The Cl atom, though not on the O–H, pulls electron density through the bonds (an inductive effect).
That helps spread the negative charge of the anion, so the acid gives up its proton more readily: about 80 times stronger.
blocks.a: The electronegative Cl stabilizes the conjugate base.

blocks.html: Saying HF is the strongest hydrohalic acid because F is the most electronegative. Electronegativity decides across a period; down a group the bond strength dominates, and the H–F bond is by far the strongest. Check: HF has $K_a = 6.8 \times 10^{-4}$, a weak acid, while HCl, HBr and HI are all strong.

blocks.html: A buffer resists changes in pH. It is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base, in comparable amounts: exactly the kind of ions you met in salt solutions. Blood, seawater and most lab reactions rely on buffers.

The weak acid HA neutralizes added base, $\mathrm{HA + OH^- \to A^- + H_2O}$, and the conjugate base $\mathrm{A^-}$ neutralizes added acid, $\mathrm{A^- + H_3O^+ \to HA + H_2O}$. Both reactions go essentially to completion, so the strong acid or base is replaced by a weak one and the pH changes only a little.

The pH of a buffer depends on the ratio $[\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]$ (as the next lesson shows). Adding a little strong acid turns a little $\mathrm{A^-}$ into HA: the ratio changes slightly, so the pH does too, but only slightly. In plain water, the same acid has nothing to react with, so it all stays as $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ and the pH crashes. A strong acid with its own salt (HCl with NaCl) cannot buffer: $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is too weak a base to take up added acid.

blocks.title: Which mixtures are buffers?
blocks.q: Which of these make a buffer: (a) HCl and NaCl; (b) $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$; (c) HF and NaF; (d) 0.20 mol $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ with 0.10 mol NaOH?
steps: (a) No: HCl is strong, and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ cannot take up acid.
(b) Yes: weak base plus its conjugate acid. (c) Yes: weak acid plus its conjugate base.
(d) Yes: the NaOH turns 0.10 mol of the acid into acetate, leaving 0.10 mol of each. A buffer can be made by half-neutralizing a weak acid.

blocks.html: Thinking a buffer keeps the pH from changing at all, or that a strong acid plus its salt makes a buffer. A buffer slows the change; enough acid or base will still overwhelm it. And it needs a weak acid with its conjugate base, so both partners can react.
Blood is held near pH 7.4 mainly by the carbonic acid / hydrogen carbonate pair, with the lungs adjusting the amount of $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
A buffer's pH depends on the ratio of base to acid. Rearranging $K_a$ and taking logarithms gives a formula that shows this directly.

$$\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$$
When the two are equal, $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a$. Every factor of 10 in the ratio moves the pH by 1.

Start from $K_a = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$ and solve for $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = K_a\dfrac{[\mathrm{HA}]}{[\mathrm{A^-}]}$. Take $-\log$ of both sides: $-\log[\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = -\log K_a - \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{HA}]}{[\mathrm{A^-}]}$, that is, $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$. In a buffer both are present in large amounts, so so little ionizes that you can use the amounts you mixed. Since both share the same volume, a ratio of moles works as well as a ratio of molarities.

blocks.html: For a base buffer you can work with $K_b$ instead: $\text{pOH} = \text{p}K_b + \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{HB^+}]}{[\mathrm{B}]}$, then $\text{pH} = 14.00 - \text{pOH}$. It gives the same answer as using the $\text{p}K_a$ of the conjugate acid, which is usually quicker. Read the other way, the equation says the $\text{p}K_a$ of an acid is the pH at which it is exactly half ionized, which is how $\text{p}K_a$ values are measured.

Putting the acid over the base inside the log, which flips the sign of the correction. Check: more base than acid must give a pH above the $\text{p}K_a$; more acid, below. Remember "base over acid," as in the order the reaction makes them.
The equation works well when both concentrations are at least about 100 times $K_a$ and the ratio is between 0.1 and 10. Outside those limits, solve the equilibrium in full.

The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation works in reverse too: given the pH of a solution, it tells you which form of an acid dominates. This is how chemists and biologists predict the charge of a molecule in a given solution.

When $\text{pH} < \text{p}K_a$, the protonated form (HA) dominates. When $\text{pH} > \text{p}K_a$, the deprotonated form ($\mathrm{A^-}$) dominates. At $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a$ they are equal, and each pH unit away from the $\text{p}K_a$ is another factor of 10 in the ratio.

From the equation, $\dfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} = 10^{\text{pH} - \text{p}K_a}$. A high pH means few protons around, so the acid has given its proton up; a low pH means plenty of protons, so the acid keeps it. The fraction in the base form is $\dfrac{1}{1 + 10^{\text{p}K_a - \text{pH}}}$.

The same rule explains indicators: an indicator is a weak acid whose two forms have different colors, so the color switches as the pH passes its $\text{p}K_a$. It also explains why many drugs are absorbed in one part of the body and not another: the uncharged form crosses cell membranes more easily, and which form dominates depends on the local pH.
Amino acids carry several groups with different $\text{p}K_a$ values, so their overall charge changes with pH. That is how proteins are separated by charge in a gel.
When strong acid or base is added to a buffer, it reacts completely with one buffer partner first. So the calculation has two stages: stoichiometry, then equilibrium.

Stage 1: work in moles. The added $\mathrm{OH^-}$ converts that many moles of HA to $\mathrm{A^-}$ (or added $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ converts $\mathrm{A^-}$ to HA). Stage 2: put the new mole ratio into $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{A^-}}}{n_\mathrm{HA}}$.

A strong base reacting with a weak acid has an enormous equilibrium constant ($K = K_a/K_w$, about $10^{9}$ for acetic acid), so it goes to completion before anything else matters. Only after that does the weak-acid equilibrium set the pH. Moles are easier than molarities here because adding a solution changes the volume, but both buffer partners share the same final volume, so the volume cancels from the ratio.

A buffer can absorb only so much. From buffer additions you saw that once one partner is used up, the pH changes fast. Two choices decide how well a buffer works: which acid, and how much of it.

Choose a weak acid whose $\text{p}K_a$ is within about 1 unit of the pH you want (ideally close to it). Its capacity, the amount of acid or base it can absorb before the pH shifts a lot, grows with the amounts of HA and $\mathrm{A^-}$ present, and is largest when they are equal.

A buffer works only while both partners are present in useful amounts. At pH = pKa they are equal, so it can absorb acid and base equally well. At $\text{p}K_a \pm 1$, one partner is ten times the other, so the buffer is lopsided. And the pH depends only on the ratio, but how much it can absorb depends on the moles: a 0.01 M buffer and a 1 M buffer can have the same pH, yet the first is used up by 1/100 as much acid.

In titration calculations you found the equivalence point. A titration curve shows the pH all the way through. For a strong acid and strong base, each point is a strong-acid or strong-base pH after the neutralization.

At each volume: find moles of acid and base, let them neutralize, and divide whatever is left over by the total volume. Before equivalence, leftover $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ sets the pH; at equivalence, the solution is neutral salt water, pH 7.00 at 25 °C; after it, leftover $\mathrm{OH^-}$ sets the pH.

$\mathrm{H_3O^+ + OH^- \to 2H_2O}$ goes to completion, so only the excess matters. Near equivalence, the excess is tiny and a single drop changes it by orders of magnitude, which is why the curve rises so steeply there. The salt formed, such as NaCl, does not react with water, so at equivalence the pH is that of pure water.

blocks.html: Why is the curve so flat at first and so steep near equivalence? The pH is a logarithm. Early on, adding base cuts the leftover acid by a small fraction, which barely moves its log. Near equivalence, a single drop can cut the leftover acid by a factor of 100 or more, and then switch the solution to excess base: the pH leaps several units. The point where an indicator changes color, the end point, is chosen to fall on that leap, so it lands within a drop of the true equivalence point.

Forgetting to add the two volumes together. After mixing, the leftover acid or base is spread through acid volume plus base volume. Check: the concentration of the excess must be smaller than either starting concentration.

Titrating a weak acid with a strong base gives a different curve from the strong–strong case. Between the start and the equivalence point the flask holds a buffer, so the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation does most of the work.

Start: weak-acid pH. Before equivalence: a buffer, $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log(n_{\mathrm{A^-}}/n_\mathrm{HA})$; at the halfway point $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a$. At equivalence: only $\mathrm{A^-}$, a weak base, so the pH is above 7. After: excess $\mathrm{OH^-}$ sets the pH.

Each portion of NaOH turns some HA into $\mathrm{A^-}$. Halfway, half is converted, so $n_{\mathrm{A^-}} = n_\mathrm{HA}$ and the log term is zero. That is how $\text{p}K_a$ values are measured. At equivalence every HA has become $\mathrm{A^-}$, which takes protons from water and makes $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so the pH is basic. The jump at equivalence is smaller than for a strong acid, because the curve starts higher.

An indicator signals the end of a titration by changing color. Picking one means matching its color change to the steep part of the titration curve.

An indicator is a weak acid, HIn, whose acid and base forms have different colors. It changes color over roughly $\text{p}K_\text{In} \pm 1$. Choose one whose range falls on the vertical jump of the curve, which contains the equivalence point.

$\dfrac{[\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]} = 10^{\text{pH} - \text{p}K_\text{In}}$. Your eye sees a mixed color only while neither form outnumbers the other by more than about 10 to 1, so the change spans about 2 pH units around $\text{p}K_\text{In}$. On the steep part of a titration curve a single drop moves the pH by several units, so an indicator anywhere on that jump changes color within a drop of the equivalence point.

blocks.html: "Insoluble" salts from precipitation reactions do dissolve a little. A saturated solution is a heterogeneous equilibrium between the solid and its ions, and its constant is the solubility product.

For $\mathrm{M}_a\mathrm{X}_b\mathrm{(s)} \rightleftharpoons a\mathrm{M}^{m+} + b\mathrm{X}^{x-}$, $K_{sp} = [\mathrm{M}^{m+}]^a[\mathrm{X}^{x-}]^b$ (the solid is left out). If $s$ is the molar solubility (moles of salt that dissolve per liter), the ions are $as$ and $bs$, so $K_{sp} = (as)^a(bs)^b$. Solve for $s$ with an nth root.

Every formula unit that dissolves puts $a$ cations and $b$ anions into solution. So if $s$ mol/L dissolve, the cation concentration is $as$ and the anion's is $bs$. For $\mathrm{PbI_2}$, one $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and two $\mathrm{I^-}$ per unit: $K_{sp} = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3$. The 2 is applied twice: once to make $[\mathrm{I^-}] = 2s$ and once as the exponent.

Solubilities calculated from $K_{sp}$ are good estimates, not exact values. In real solutions some ions pair up, some react with water (carbonate and phosphate are bases), and crowded ions behave as if they were less concentrated. These effects are small for salts like AgCl and larger for salts with highly charged or basic ions.
Molar solubility times molar mass gives grams per liter. For AgCl: $(1.3 \times 10^{-5})(143.3) = 1.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{g/L}$, about 2 mg in a liter.

blocks.html: A smaller Ksp usually suggests a less soluble salt. But that comparison is fair only when the salts break into the same number of ions.
For salts with the same ion pattern (both 1:1, or both 1:2), the smaller $K_{sp}$ is the less soluble salt. For different patterns, compute each molar solubility $s$ and compare those instead.

$K_{sp}$ is $s^2$ for a 1:1 salt but $4s^3$ for a 1:2 salt: different powers of $s$. Since $s$ is a small number, its cube is far smaller than its square. A 1:2 salt can therefore have a smaller $K_{sp}$ than a 1:1 salt and still dissolve more.

blocks.html: Le Chatelier’s principle applies to dissolving too. If the water already contains one of a salt's ions, the solubility equilibrium is pushed back toward the solid, and less of the salt dissolves. This is the Q-and-K argument once more.

In a solution that already holds an ion at concentration $c$, set up $K_{sp}$ with that ion at $c$ plus what the salt adds. When $c$ is much larger than what the salt adds, use $c$ alone: for a 1:1 salt, $s = K_{sp}/c$.

Adding $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ to saturated AgCl raises $Q = [\mathrm{Ag^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]$ above $K_{sp}$, so AgCl precipitates until $Q = K_{sp}$ again. In a solution that starts with $0.10\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $[\mathrm{Ag^+}]$ can reach only $K_{sp}/0.10$ before the product hits the limit. The salt's own contribution to $[\mathrm{Cl^-}]$ is then negligible.

blocks.html: Chemists use the common-ion effect on purpose. To remove a metal ion from solution as completely as possible, they add a modest excess of the precipitating ion: the extra anion pushes the leftover metal ion concentration far below what it would be in a saturated solution of the pure salt.

Using the molar solubility in pure water even when a common ion is already present. The ion already in solution counts in $K_{sp}$. Check: the solubility with a common ion must come out smaller than in pure water.

blocks.html: Will a solid form when two solutions are mixed? Compare the reaction quotient of the ions with Ksp. The one step people skip is dilution: after mixing, every ion is in a larger volume.

Find each ion's concentration after mixing, $c = \dfrac{c_0V_0}{V_\text{total}}$. Compute $Q$ the same way as $K_{sp}$. If $Q > K_{sp}$, a precipitate forms; if $Q < K_{sp}$, it does not; if $Q = K_{sp}$, the solution is just saturated.

$Q$ above $K_{sp}$ means more ions are in solution than the equilibrium allows, so some combine into solid until the product drops back to $K_{sp}$. Below $K_{sp}$, the solution is unsaturated and more solid could even dissolve.

blocks.html: Some salts dissolve far better in acid. The reason combines the common-ion idea with ions that are weak bases: acid removes a basic anion from the solution, and the solid dissolves to replace it.

If a salt's anion is a weak base ($\mathrm{OH^-}$, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{F^-}$, $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$, $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$), lowering the pH raises its solubility. If the anion is the conjugate base of a strong acid ($\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{Br^-}$, $\mathrm{I^-}$), pH has essentially no effect.

For $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2(s) \rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+} + 2OH^-}$, acid reacts with the hydroxide: $\mathrm{OH^- + H_3O^+ \to 2H_2O}$. That lowers $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, $Q$ falls below $K_{sp}$, and more solid dissolves. Carbonate reacts with acid to give $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ and then $\mathrm{CO_2}$ gas, which leaves entirely. But $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ will not take a proton in water (HCl is strong), so acid cannot pull AgCl apart.

blocks.title: Magnesium hydroxide at two pH values
blocks.q: $K_{sp}$ of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ is $5.6 \times 10^{-12}$. Find its molar solubility in solutions buffered at pH 10.00 and pH 9.00.
steps: At pH 10.00: pOH 4.00, $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ (fixed by the buffer). $$s = [\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}] = \dfrac{5.6 \times 10^{-12}}{(1.0 \times 10^{-4})^2} = 5.6 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M}$$
One pH unit lower, 100 times more dissolves (because $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ is squared).

blocks.title: Which salts care about pH?
blocks.q: Which become more soluble in acid: $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, AgCl, $\mathrm{CaF_2}$, AgBr, $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$?
steps: Basic anions: $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{F^-}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$. Those salts dissolve better in acid.
$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ come from strong acids and do not react with $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$.

blocks.html: Tooth enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, $\mathrm{Ca_5(PO_4)_3OH}$. Acids made by mouth bacteria react with its hydroxide and phosphate ions and dissolve it. Fluoride swaps in for the hydroxide to form fluorapatite, which resists acid better. Limestone caves form the same way: rainwater with dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is slightly acidic and slowly dissolves calcium carbonate.

The same reasoning explains why some metal sulfides dissolve in acid and others do not: sulfide is a strong base, and acid pulls it out of solution as $\mathrm{HS^-}$ and $\mathrm{H_2S}$. Chemists separate metal ions this way by controlling the pH.

Expecting pH to change the solubility of every salt, including chlorides, bromides and iodides. Only anions that are weak bases react with $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$. Check: is the anion the partner of a strong acid? If so, pH does not matter.

blocks.html: A lone pair can do more than sit on an atom: it can form a bond to something that has room for it. That broader idea of acids and bases explains why metal ions grab ammonia or cyanide, and why that makes some insoluble salts dissolve.

A Lewis base donates an electron pair; a Lewis acid accepts one. Metal ions are Lewis acids. A metal ion bonded to several Lewis bases (ligands) is a complex ion, such as $\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}$. Its formation constant $K_f$ measures how tightly it holds together, and forming it can dissolve a salt: $K = K_{sp} \times K_f$.

$\mathrm{BF_3}$ has only six electrons around boron and an empty orbital, so it accepts the lone pair of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ with no proton involved. A metal ion's empty orbitals accept lone pairs the same way. When ammonia ties up $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ as $\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}$, free $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ drops, $Q$ falls below $K_{sp}$ for AgCl, and more AgCl dissolves. Adding the two reactions multiplies their constants.
