blocks.html: The first law says energy is conserved, but it does not say which way things go. Heat flows from hot to cold, gases spread out, ice melts in a warm room, and never the reverse on their own. The quantity that tracks this direction is entropy, and it comes from counting. You will need logarithms.

A microstate is one specific arrangement of all the particles and their energy. $W$ is the number of microstates that look the same from outside. Entropy is $S = k\ln W$, with $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}$ (Boltzmann's constant). Systems drift toward the conditions with the most microstates, so entropy tends to increase.

Every microstate is equally likely. Put 4 gas molecules in a box with two halves: there are $2^4 = 16$ microstates. Only 1 has all four on the left, but 6 have two on each side. So the spread-out state is 6 times more likely than the bunched-up one. With $6 \times 10^{23}$ molecules, the odds against all of them gathering on one side are beyond astronomical, which is why it never happens. The logarithm makes entropy add up properly: two systems together have $W = W_1W_2$, so $S = S_1 + S_2$.

blocks.name: ch-microstates
blocks.cap: Ten particles in a box with a divider. Count the ways to have k on the left: the even split has by far the most arrangements.

blocks.title: Counting arrangements
blocks.q: Ten gas molecules move freely in a box. What is the chance that all ten are in the left half at once? How many microstates have exactly five on each side?
steps: Each molecule has 2 choices, so there are $2^{10} = 1024$ microstates in all.
All on the left: 1 microstate, a chance of $1/1024$.
Five and five: choose which 5 are on the left, $\binom{10}{5} = 252$ microstates (about 25% of all).

blocks.title: A gas doubling its volume
blocks.q: One mole of an ideal gas expands into a vacuum, doubling its volume. Find $\Delta S$.
steps: Each molecule now has twice as many places to be, so $W$ is multiplied by $2^{N_A}$.
$\Delta S = k\ln(2^{N_A}) = N_Ak\ln 2 = R\ln 2$, since $N_Ak = R$.
$\Delta S = (8.314)(0.693) = 5.76\ \text{J/K}$. No heat flowed and no energy changed, yet entropy rose.

blocks.name: ch-microstates
blocks.cap: Two small solids sharing six quanta of energy. Starting with all the energy in A, the most likely split spreads it over both: that spreading is heat flowing from hot to cold.

blocks.html: Thinking of entropy only as messiness. Messiness misleads: two gases mixing and energy spreading from a hot object to a cold one both raise entropy, though neither looks messier. Check: ask how many ways the particles and the energy can be arranged.
Count arrangements yourself, and watch heat flow from hot to cold by pure chance, in the Science Lab's Entropy and the Second Law chapter.
With microstates in mind, you can predict whether a process raises or lowers entropy without any numbers. More freedom of motion and more ways to share energy mean more microstates.

$\Delta S > 0$ when the moles of gas increase, when a solid melts or a liquid boils, when a solid dissolves (usually), when a substance warms, and when gases or liquids mix. The biggest effect by far is a change in the moles of gas.

Gas molecules range over the whole container, so a gas has vastly more positions available than a liquid, and a liquid more than a solid. A warmer substance has more energy to share among its particles, so more ways to share it. Dissolving breaks a crystal's order and lets ions move through the solvent (although small, highly charged ions can order the water around them enough to make $\Delta S$ negative).

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: Water as a solid, liquid and gas. Each step frees the molecules to more positions and motions, so entropy rises from left to right.

blocks.title: Count only the gas
blocks.q: Predict the sign of $\Delta S$ for $\mathrm{2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \to 2H_2O(l)}$.
steps: Moles of gas: 3 on the left, 0 on the right.
Three moles of gas become a liquid: a large drop in entropy. $\Delta S < 0$.

blocks.title: Four quick predictions
blocks.q: Give the sign of $\Delta S$: (a) $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) \to CaO(s) + CO_2(g)}$; (b) $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \to 2NH_3(g)}$; (c) $\mathrm{2H_2O_2(l) \to 2H_2O(l) + O_2(g)}$; (d) $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ at 20 °C warmed to 60 °C.
steps: (a) A gas forms from a solid: positive.
(c) A gas forms from liquids: positive. (d) Warming: positive.

blocks.html: When the moles of gas do not change, the sign is harder to call by eye, and $\Delta S$ is usually small. Then you need the tabulated values of the next lesson.

Counting all the moles in an equation instead of only the moles of gas. In $\mathrm{C(s) + O_2(g) \to CO_2(g)}$ the moles go from 2 to 1, but the moles of gas stay at 1, and $\Delta S$ is in fact slightly positive. Check: tally (g) species only.
To put numbers on entropy changes, chemists tabulate standard molar entropies, $S^\circ$. You combine them the way you combined enthalpies of formation, with one important difference.

The third law: a perfect crystal at $0\ \text{K}$ has $S = 0$. So every substance, element or compound, has a positive absolute entropy $S^\circ$ at $298\ \text{K}$. For a reaction, $$\Delta S^\circ = \sum nS^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum nS^\circ(\text{reactants})$$

A perfect crystal at absolute zero has only one possible arrangement: $W = 1$, so $S = k\ln 1 = 0$. That gives entropy a true zero point. Warming a substance from there adds microstates, so $S^\circ$ at $298\ \text{K}$ is measured from heat capacities as an absolute value. Enthalpy has no such zero, which is why $\Delta H^\circ_f$ of an element is defined as zero; $S^\circ$ of an element is not zero at all.

blocks.html: Three trends make the table easy to read. Gases have much larger $S^\circ$ than liquids, and liquids than solids. Within one phase, larger and more complex molecules have larger entropies (more ways to vibrate and rotate): $S^\circ$ rises from $\mathrm{CH_4}$ (186.3) to $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ (229.2) to $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$ (270.3). And hard, tightly bonded solids such as diamond (2.4) have very low entropies, while soft solids such as lead (64.8) have higher ones.

blocks.html: Some processes lower the system's entropy and happen anyway: water freezes, and ammonia forms from a reaction with ΔS° = −198 J/K. The second law explains this by counting the surroundings too.

Second law: a process is thermodynamically favored (spontaneous) when the entropy of the universe increases: $\Delta S_\text{univ} = \Delta S_\text{sys} + \Delta S_\text{surr} > 0$. At constant temperature and pressure, the surroundings gain entropy from the heat the system releases: $\Delta S_\text{surr} = -\dfrac{\Delta H_\text{sys}}{T}$.

When a reaction releases heat, that energy spreads into the surroundings and gives them more ways to share energy, raising their entropy. The same amount of heat matters more when the surroundings are cold: adding 1 kJ to a cold body raises its entropy more than adding it to a hot one, because the cold body had fewer ways to share energy to begin with. So the entropy gain is the heat divided by $T$. The minus sign appears because heat released by the system ($\Delta H < 0$) is heat gained by the surroundings.

blocks.name: ch-microstates
blocks.cap: Energy shared between two solids. The total count of arrangements, $W_A \times W_B$, is largest when the energy is spread out; that is why heat flows from hot to cold.

blocks.title: Water freezing
blocks.q: For water, $\Delta H_\text{fus} = 6.01\ \text{kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S_\text{fus} = 22.0\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$. Is freezing favored at $-10\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and at $+10\ ^\circ\text{C}$?
steps: At $283\ \text{K}$: $\Delta S_\text{surr} = \dfrac{6010}{283} = +21.2\ \text{J/K}$; $\Delta S_\text{univ} = -22.0 + 21.2 = -0.8\ \text{J/K}$. Not favored: ice melts instead.
At $273\ \text{K}$ the two cancel: ice and water are in equilibrium at the melting point.

blocks.title: Making ammonia
blocks.q: At $298\ \text{K}$, $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3}$ has $\Delta H^\circ = -91.8\ \text{kJ}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -198.1\ \text{J/K}$. Is it favored?

blocks.html: Judging whether a process is favored from the system's entropy alone. Freezing and ammonia synthesis both lower the system's entropy, yet each can be favored because the heat released raises the surroundings' entropy more. Check: always add $-\Delta H/T$ before deciding.
"Spontaneous" in thermodynamics means favored, not fast. Whether it happens at a noticeable rate is a question of kinetics.
The Science Lab's Entropy and the Second Law chapter lets you run a gas backward and see why the reverse never happens on its own.

blocks.html: The second law asks you to track both the system and the surroundings. Gibbs free energy packs both into one quantity that belongs to the system alone, so you can decide from $\Delta H$, $\Delta S$ and $T$ directly.

$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ (at constant temperature and pressure). $\Delta G < 0$: thermodynamically favored. $\Delta G > 0$: not favored (the reverse is). $\Delta G = 0$: at equilibrium. Standard values add like enthalpies: $$\Delta G^\circ = \sum n\Delta G^\circ_f(\text{products}) - \sum n\Delta G^\circ_f(\text{reactants})$$

Start from $\Delta S_\text{univ} = \Delta S - \dfrac{\Delta H}{T}$. Multiply by $-T$: $-T\Delta S_\text{univ} = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. Call this $\Delta G$. Since $T$ is positive, $\Delta S_\text{univ} > 0$ exactly when $\Delta G < 0$. $\Delta G$ also means something physical: it is the most useful (non-expansion) work the process can deliver, as electrical work in a battery or chemical work in a cell.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $\Delta G^\circ$ for making ammonia against temperature (treating $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ as constant). It is negative at room temperature and crosses zero near 463 K.

blocks.title: From ΔH and ΔS
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3}$, $\Delta H^\circ = -91.8\ \text{kJ}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -198.1\ \text{J/K}$. Find $\Delta G^\circ$ at $298\ \text{K}$.
steps: Negative: favored at 298 K. The favorable $\Delta H$ outweighs the unfavorable $\Delta S$.

blocks.q: Find $\Delta G^\circ$ for $$\mathrm{CH_4(g)} + \mathrm{2O_2(g)} \to \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + \mathrm{2H_2O(l)}$$ given $\Delta G^\circ_f$: $\mathrm{CH_4}$ $-50.5$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ $-394.4$, $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ $-237.1\ \text{kJ/mol}$.
steps: Reactants: $-50.5 + 0 = -50.5\ \text{kJ}$ ($\mathrm{O_2}$ is an element in its standard state).

blocks.title: A different temperature
blocks.q: Using the same $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$, is ammonia synthesis favored at $1000\ \text{K}$?
steps: Positive: at 1000 K the entropy term wins and ammonia tends to decompose. (This assumes $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ stay about the same when heated, which is a fair first estimate.)

blocks.html: Combining $\Delta H$ in kJ with $\Delta S$ in J/K without converting. $\Delta S$ values are about a thousand times smaller in kJ, so skipping the conversion makes $T\Delta S$ a thousand times too large. Check: write the units on every term; $T\Delta S$ must come out in kJ.

The superscript ° means standard conditions: 1 bar for gases and 1 M for solutes. In a real mixture the free energy change is $\Delta G$, which can differ from $\Delta G^\circ$; the lesson on free energy and equilibrium shows how.
Unlike $S^\circ$, $\Delta G^\circ_f$ of an element in its standard state is zero, just as for $\Delta H^\circ_f$.
In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, temperature multiplies only the entropy term. So the signs of $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ decide whether heating helps or hurts, and where the switch happens.

When $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ have opposite effects, the process is favored on one side of a crossover temperature $T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$ (with consistent units), where $\Delta G = 0$. Endothermic with $\Delta S > 0$: favored above it. Exothermic with $\Delta S < 0$: favored below it.

At low temperature, $T\Delta S$ is small and $\Delta H$ decides. At high temperature, $T\Delta S$ dominates and $\Delta S$ decides. Setting $\Delta G = 0$ gives the balance point. This treats $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ as roughly constant over the range, which is a good first estimate.

$T = \dfrac{-91\,800\ \text{J}}{-198.1\ \text{J/K}} = 463\ \text{K}$. Below about 463 K (190 °C) the reaction is favored under standard conditions.

blocks.html: This is why the Haber process has to balance two needs: the reaction is favored only at lower temperatures, but it is fast enough only at higher ones (with a catalyst).

Thinking an endothermic reaction can never be favored. If $\Delta S$ is positive, heating makes $T\Delta S$ win: ice melts and limestone decomposes, both endothermic. Check the sign of $\Delta S$ before ruling a reaction out.
A negative ΔG says a reaction can happen; it does not say when. The rate depends on the activation barrier, which thermodynamics does not see.

Thermodynamics (ΔG) tells you which direction is favored and how far a reaction can go. Kinetics ($E_a$) tells you how fast. A favored reaction with a high barrier can be so slow that it effectively never happens: it is under kinetic control. When two products can form, the one with the lower barrier may form first even if the other is more stable.

$\Delta G$ depends only on the start and end states. The rate depends on the height of the hump between them, through $e^{-E_a/RT}$. Nothing links the two: a reaction can fall a long way downhill and still have a high wall to climb first.

blocks.title: Diamonds are not forever
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{C(diamond) \to C(graphite)}$, $\Delta G^\circ = -2.9\ \text{kJ/mol}$ at 25 °C. Why do diamonds last?
steps: $\Delta G^\circ < 0$: graphite is the more stable form, so the change is favored.
But turning diamond into graphite means breaking and rearranging strong C–C bonds throughout the crystal, a huge barrier. At room temperature the rate is immeasurably small.
blocks.a: The conversion is favored but kinetically blocked.

blocks.title: Two products, two barriers
blocks.q: A reactant can form P1 (barrier 60 kJ/mol) or P2 (barrier 80 kJ/mol); P2 is more stable. At 298 K, roughly how much faster does P1 form, if the factors $A$ are equal?
steps: About 3200 times faster. If P1 cannot easily turn back, the mixture ends up mostly P1, the kinetic product, even though P2 is thermodynamically favored.

items: Wood and paper are favored to burn in air, but need a flame to get over the barrier.
Hydrogen and oxygen sit unchanged until a spark: $\Delta G^\circ = -237\ \text{kJ}$ per mole of water.
Your body's molecules are not at equilibrium with oxygen; enzymes choose which favored reactions run, and when.

blocks.html: The reverse is true too: a fast reaction need not be favored. Thermodynamics and kinetics answer different questions, and a full description of a reaction needs both.

Thinking a thermodynamically favored reaction must be fast, as if $\Delta G$ set the rate. $\Delta G$ fixes the direction; $E_a$ sets the speed. Check: look for the activation energy (or a catalyst) before predicting how fast anything goes.
Both $\Delta G^\circ$ and K describe how far a reaction goes, so they must be linked. The link is logarithmic, so you will solve log equations with it.

$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, and at equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K$, so
$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K, \qquad K = e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}$$
with $R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$ and $\Delta G^\circ$ in J/mol. Negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K > 1$.

$\Delta G^\circ$ is the free-energy change when everything is in its standard state ($Q = 1$). For any other mixture, $RT\ln Q$ corrects it: too much product (large $Q$) makes $\Delta G$ less negative. As the reaction runs, $Q$ moves toward $K$ and $\Delta G$ moves toward zero. When $\Delta G$ reaches zero there is no more drive either way: that is equilibrium. Setting $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K$ gives the relation.

blocks.html: Combining $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$ with $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ gives $\ln K = -\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + \dfrac{\Delta S^\circ}{R}$. For an exothermic reaction, $K$ falls as $T$ rises; for an endothermic one, it grows. This is the quantitative form of Le Chatelier’s rule for temperature.
For reactions in solution, $K$ uses concentrations; for gases, partial pressures. Either way the activities in $Q$ and $K$ are pure numbers, so the logarithm makes sense.

Thinking $\Delta G^\circ$ is zero at equilibrium. It is $\Delta G$ that reaches zero; $\Delta G^\circ$ is a fixed number for the reaction at a given temperature, and it sets where equilibrium lies. Check: if $\Delta G^\circ$ were zero, $K$ would be exactly 1.
Living cells build proteins and sugars, and both have positive ΔG. They manage it by pairing each uphill reaction with a strongly downhill one. Free energies add the way enthalpies do in Hess’s law.

When two reactions share an intermediate and run as one combined process, their free energies add: $\Delta G_\text{total} = \Delta G_1 + \Delta G_2$, and their constants multiply: $K_\text{total} = K_1K_2$. If the total is negative, the combined process is favored, even though one part alone is not.

$G$ is a state function, so the overall change does not depend on the path; adding the equations adds the $\Delta G$ values. Coupling is not a bookkeeping trick: the two reactions must be physically linked, usually through a shared intermediate. In cells, ATP transfers a phosphate group to the reactant, making an activated intermediate whose next step is downhill.

steps: $K > 1$, so $\Delta G^\circ < 0$: the coupled process is favored.

blocks.html: The $\circ\prime$ (degree-prime) marks the biochemists' standard state: pH 7 rather than $1\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$, which suits reactions in cells. Other values you will meet: phosphoenolpyruvate hydrolysis, $-61.9\ \text{kJ/mol}$; glucose + phosphate → glucose 6-phosphate, $+13.8\ \text{kJ/mol}$. Industry couples reactions too: in smelting, carbon's reaction with oxygen pays for pulling oxygen out of a metal oxide.
A typical cell turns over its ATP many times a day, remaking it from ADP and phosphate with energy from food; the ATP is a carrier of free energy, not a store.

Thinking coupling changes the $\Delta G$ of the unfavored step itself. That step still has $\Delta G = +14.2\ \text{kJ/mol}$; what changes is that it no longer runs alone. Check: the total is the sum, and each part keeps its own value.

When zinc metal sits in copper sulfate solution, copper plates out and the zinc dissolves: a redox reaction, as in balancing redox equations. The electrons pass straight from zinc atoms to copper ions, and the energy only warms the solution. Separate the two half-reactions, connect them with a wire, and those same electrons do useful work on the way. That is a galvanic (voltaic) cell.

Oxidation happens at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Electrons flow through the external wire from anode to cathode. A salt bridge (or porous barrier) lets ions move between the two solutions to keep each one neutral: anions drift toward the anode, cations toward the cathode. In a galvanic cell, the anode is the negative terminal.

At the zinc electrode, $\mathrm{Zn \to Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$ leaves electrons behind in the metal, so it becomes the negative terminal. At the copper electrode, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \to Cu}$ takes electrons from the metal. Without the salt bridge, positive charge would pile up in the zinc solution and negative charge in the copper solution, and the current would stop almost at once. Ions moving through the bridge carry the charge inside the cell; electrons cannot travel through water.

How much voltage does a galvanic cell give? Each half-cell has a tendency to be reduced, measured as a standard reduction potential. Subtracting two of them gives the cell's voltage.

$E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode}$, using standard reduction potentials for both (1 M solutions, 1 bar gases, 25 °C). A positive $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ means the reaction as written is favored. $E^\circ$ is never multiplied by a coefficient, even when a half-reaction is multiplied to balance electrons.

Only differences in potential can be measured, so one half-cell is chosen as zero: the standard hydrogen electrode, $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \to H_2}$, $E^\circ = 0$. Everything else is measured against it. A higher (more positive) $E^\circ$ means a stronger pull on electrons, so the half-cell with the higher value becomes the cathode. Potential is energy per unit charge (volts are joules per coulomb). Doubling the amount of reaction doubles both the energy and the charge, so the ratio stays the same: $E^\circ$ is intensive, like temperature.

blocks.html: A cell's voltage, ΔG° and $K$ all measure how far a reaction wants to go, so each can be computed from the others. Standard potentials are often the easiest of the three to look up.

$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$, where $n$ is the moles of electrons transferred in the balanced equation and $F = 96\,485\ \text{C/mol}$. Combined with $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$: $\ln K = \dfrac{nFE^\circ}{RT}$, or at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.0592\ \text{V}}$.

Electrical work is charge times voltage. Moving $n$ moles of electrons (charge $nF$) through a potential difference $E$ can do $nFE$ joules of work, the most useful work the reaction can give, which is $-\Delta G$. Setting the two expressions for $\Delta G^\circ$ equal gives $RT\ln K = nFE^\circ$. At 298 K, $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0592\ \text{V}$.

Add the free energies instead. For example, $\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^- \to Fe^{2+}}$ ($+0.77\ \text{V}$) and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \to Fe}$ ($-0.45\ \text{V}$) give $\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + 3e^- \to Fe}$ with $E^\circ = \dfrac{1(0.77) + 2(-0.45)}{3} = -0.04\ \text{V}$, not $0.32\ \text{V}$.
A large positive $E^\circ$ says a reaction is favored, not that it is fast. Some favored electrode reactions, like making oxygen from water, need extra voltage to run at a useful rate.

blocks.html: Standard potentials assume 1 M solutions. Real cells drift away from that as they run, and their voltage changes. Combining ΔG = −nFE with ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q gives the correction.

$$E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$$ or, at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $$E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0592\ \text{V}}{n}\log Q$$
$Q$ is products over reactants, with solids left out. As the cell runs, $Q$ grows toward $K$ and $E$ falls toward zero: a dead battery is a cell at equilibrium.

Substitute $\Delta G = -nFE$ and $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ into $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ and divide by $-nF$. When products are scarce ($Q < 1$), the log is negative and $E$ is larger than $E^\circ$; when products have built up, $E$ is smaller. At equilibrium $Q = K$ and $E = 0$.

Putting the reactant concentrations on top of $Q$, or including solids. $Q$ has the same form as $K$: products over reactants, aqueous ions and gases only. Check: making more reactant should raise the voltage; if your $Q$ says otherwise, it is upside down.

A pH meter uses the same law. Its glass electrode responds to $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, and at 25 °C its voltage changes by about $0.0592\ \text{V}$ (59 mV) for each unit of pH, the Nernst slope for one electron per proton. That is why meters are calibrated with buffers of known pH, and why they correct for temperature.
Your nerve cells use concentration differences the same way: a membrane potential of roughly $-70\ \text{mV}$ comes mainly from a difference in potassium ion concentration across the cell membrane.

blocks.html: A negative cell potential means a reaction will not run on its own. An outside power source can force it: that is electrolysis, used to make aluminum, chlorine and sodium hydroxide, and to plate metals.

In an electrolytic cell, a power supply pushes electrons into one electrode, making it the negative cathode, where reduction happens. The other electrode, connected to the positive terminal, is the anode, where oxidation happens. The applied voltage must be at least the size of the (negative) cell potential, and in practice more.

Anode always means oxidation and cathode always means reduction, in every cell. What differs is the source of the push. In a galvanic cell, the reaction itself makes the anode negative by leaving electrons there. In an electrolytic cell, the power supply drags electrons out of the anode, so it is positive, and pumps them into the cathode, which is negative. The extra voltage beyond the minimum (the overpotential) is needed to drive the reactions at a useful rate.

Recharging a battery is electrolysis: the charger pushes the battery's reaction backward, restoring its reactants.

Thinking the anode is negative in every cell. It is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in an electrolytic cell. Check: the anode is always where oxidation happens; the sign follows from what drives the electrons.

Electrolysis is stoichiometry with electrons as a reactant. The current tells you how many electrons pass, and the half-reaction tells you how many each ion needs. From there, moles to grams as usual. This builds on electrolytic cells.

Charge $q = It$ (coulombs = amperes × seconds). Moles of electrons $= q/F$, with $F = 96\,485\ \text{C/mol}$. Moles of product = moles of electrons ÷ electrons per formula (from the half-reaction). Mass = moles × molar mass.

An ampere is one coulomb per second, so current times time is total charge. One mole of electrons carries $96\,485\ \text{C}$ (Faraday's constant, $N_A$ times the charge of one electron). Each $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ needs two electrons to become a copper atom, so a mole of electrons makes only half a mole of copper. Michael Faraday found this pattern by experiment in the 1830s: the same charge always deposits amounts of different metals in proportion to molar mass divided by ionic charge.

blocks.html: Battery capacity is often given in ampere-hours, a unit of charge: $1\ \text{A·h} = 3600\ \text{C}$. A phone battery rated $3.0\ \text{A·h}$ can deliver $10\,800\ \text{C}$, about $0.11\ \text{mol}$ of electrons, before it needs recharging.

In practice some current is lost to side reactions, such as making hydrogen at the cathode, so real yields are slightly below the Faraday's-law amount. Industry reports this as the current efficiency.

Forgetting how many electrons each ion needs, which predicts twice as much copper as can form. Check the half-reaction every time: $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ takes 1, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ takes 2, $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ takes 3.
Every battery is a galvanic cell built to be portable, and rust is a galvanic cell nobody wanted. Both come down to which metal is oxidized and where the electrons go.

A battery stores chemicals that react to push electrons through a circuit; recharging runs the reaction backward with outside power. Corrosion of iron is oxidation of the metal by oxygen in the presence of water. A more active metal (lower $E^\circ$), such as zinc or magnesium, can protect iron by being oxidized in its place.

A battery does not hold a supply of electrons; it holds two substances that want to exchange electrons, kept apart so the exchange can happen only through your device. When one of them runs out, the voltage drops. In rusting, one region of the iron acts as an anode ($\mathrm{Fe \to Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$) and another as a cathode where oxygen is reduced ($\mathrm{O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^- \to 2H_2O}$); the water film acts as the salt bridge, which is why salt speeds rust. If a more active metal touches the iron, it becomes the anode instead, and the iron is protected.

blocks.html: In radioactive decay you met alpha, beta and gamma radiation. Now the question is which nuclei decay, and how. The answer comes from the balance between protons and neutrons.

Stable nuclei lie in a narrow band of stability: $N/Z \approx 1$ for light elements, rising to about 1.5 for the heaviest. A nucleus above the band (too many neutrons) undergoes beta decay, $\mathrm{n \to p + e^-}$. A nucleus below it (too few neutrons) undergoes positron emission, $\mathrm{p \to n + e^+}$, or electron capture, $\mathrm{p + e^- \to n}$. Every nucleus with $Z > 83$ is unstable, and heavy ones usually alpha decay.

Two forces compete. The strong nuclear force attracts every nucleon to its close neighbors, protons and neutrons alike, but reaches only about the width of a nucleon. The electric repulsion between protons reaches across the whole nucleus, so in a big nucleus every proton pushes on every other. Extra neutrons add attraction without adding repulsion, which is why heavy stable nuclei need more neutrons than protons. Beyond bismuth, no number of neutrons is enough. A nucleus off the band moves toward it: beta decay turns a neutron into a proton (lowering $N/Z$), while positron emission and electron capture do the reverse.

steps: $Z = 6$, $N = 14 - 6 = 8$: $N/Z = 1.33$. Carbon's stable isotopes, C-12 and C-13, have 6 and 7 neutrons, so C-14 has too many.
Beta decay turns a neutron into a proton: $Z$ goes from 6 to 7, $A$ stays 14.

It needs to turn a proton into a neutron: positron emission (its main mode) or electron capture. $Z$ drops to 8.

The equation: $$ {}^{18}_{9}\mathrm{F} \to {}^{18}_{8}\mathrm{O} + {}^{0}_{+1}\mathrm{e}$$ The positron meets an electron in the body, and the two gamma rays from that meeting are what the scanner detects.

Nuclei with even numbers of both protons and neutrons are especially common among stable ones, and so are nuclei with 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82 or 126 protons or neutrons (the "magic numbers"), which fill nuclear shells.

blocks.html: Weigh a helium-4 atom and compare it with two hydrogen atoms plus two neutrons: the atom is lighter. The missing mass became the energy that holds the nucleus together, by $E = mc^2$. This connects stability with the energy of fission and fusion, and uses scientific notation throughout.

Mass defect: $\Delta m = Z\,m(^1\mathrm{H}) + N\,m_n - m(\text{atom})$. Binding energy: $E_b = \Delta mc^2$, which is $931.5\ \text{MeV}$ for every $1\ \text{u}$ of mass defect. Binding energy per nucleon, $E_b/A$, measures how tightly a nucleus is held; it peaks near iron and nickel at about $8.8\ \text{MeV}$.

Bound systems have less energy than their separate parts: energy is released when they form, and must be supplied to pull them apart. Relativity says energy has mass, so the bound nucleus weighs less. Using hydrogen-1 atoms (a proton plus an electron) instead of bare protons means the electrons are counted on both sides, so atomic masses from tables can be used directly. Because $E_b/A$ peaks near $A = 56$–62, fusing light nuclei moves up the curve and releases energy, and so does splitting heavy ones.

blocks.html: Every radioactive nucleus has the same chance of decaying in the next second, whatever its age. That is exactly a first-order process, so the equations you know apply directly, and they explain the half-lives you met before.

$N = N_0e^{-kt}$, $\ln\dfrac{N_0}{N} = kt$, and $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$, constant for each isotope. Activity (decays per second, in becquerels) is $A = kN$, so it falls by the same law. These work at any time, not just at whole numbers of half-lives.

A nucleus has no memory and no timer. In any short time interval $dt$, each one has the same small probability $k\,dt$ of decaying. So the number that decay is proportional to the number present: $-dN/dt = kN$. That is the first-order rate law, and its solution is the exponential. Temperature, pressure and chemical bonding have essentially no effect on $k$, because the nucleus is shielded by its electrons.

Living things keep a steady carbon-14 level by exchanging carbon with the air; after death the C-14 decays without being replaced. The measured half-life is about 5700 years (many older books use 5730), and real radiocarbon ages are corrected with calibration curves because the level in the air has varied a little over time.

blocks.html: In complex ions a metal ion accepts electron pairs from several Lewis bases at once. Compounds that contain such complexes are coordination compounds. To describe one, you need its parts, its coordination number and the metal's oxidation number.

The metal and its bonded ligands form the coordination sphere, written in square brackets; counter ions outside the brackets balance the charge. The coordination number is the number of donor atoms bonded to the metal (2, 4 and 6 are most common). The metal's oxidation state follows from charge balance: metal + ligand charges = charge of the complex.

Each ligand donates at least one lone pair, and each donated pair is one bond to the metal. A monodentate ligand ($\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{CN^-}$) uses one donor atom. A bidentate ligand such as ethylenediamine ($\mathrm{H_2NCH_2CH_2NH_2}$, "en") or oxalate ($\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$) grips with two, forming a ring with the metal; EDTA uses six. So the coordination number counts donor atoms, not ligands. Six donors usually sit at the corners of an octahedron; four sit at the corners of a tetrahedron or a square.

blocks.title: Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}$, find the charge of the complex ion, the oxidation state of cobalt and the coordination number.
steps: Two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ counter ions outside the brackets: total $-2$, so the complex is $+2$.
Inside: five neutral $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and one $\mathrm{Cl^-}$. $x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2$, so $x = +3$.
Six donor atoms (5 N and 1 Cl): coordination number 6.

steps: Each oxalate binds through two O atoms: $3 \times 2 = 6$ donor atoms.

steps: Only what is outside the brackets separates; the ligands stay bound.
Alfred Werner used exactly these counts, from electrical conductivity and from how much chloride precipitated with silver nitrate, to work out the structures in the 1890s.

blocks.html: Counting every atom of a ligand as a bond to the metal (so that $\mathrm{NH_3}$ would count 4), or ignoring the ligands' charges when finding the metal's oxidation state. Only donor atoms bond to the metal, and chloride, cyanide and oxalate all carry charge. Check: metal charge plus ligand charges must equal the bracket's charge, and counter ions must make the whole compound neutral.

blocks.html: Once you can find the parts of a coordination compound, its name follows a fixed recipe. The name tells a chemist every ligand, the metal and its oxidation state.

Name the cation first, then the anion, as for any salt. Inside the complex: ligands in alphabetical order (ignoring number prefixes), each with a prefix for how many (di-, tri-, tetra-; or bis-, tris- for ligands like ethylenediamine), then the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals. If the complex is an anion, the metal takes the ending -ate.

The rules make every name unique and reversible: from the name you can write the formula, and back. Anionic ligands end in -o (current IUPAC names end in -ido: chlorido, cyanido; older books use chloro, cyano). Neutral ligands have special names: ammine ($\mathrm{NH_3}$), aqua ($\mathrm{H_2O}$), carbonyl (CO). The -ate ending signals a negative complex, just as sulfate and nitrate are anions. Some -ate names use the Latin root: ferrate (Fe), cuprate (Cu), argentate (Ag), plumbate (Pb), aurate (Au), stannate (Sn).

blocks.html: Two complexes can contain exactly the same atoms and still be different compounds, because the ligands sit in different places around the metal. Using the shapes from coordination compounds, you can count these isomers.

Geometric isomers differ in which positions like ligands occupy: cis (side by side, 90° apart) or trans (opposite, 180°); in octahedra with three of a kind, fac (all on one face) or mer (around a meridian). Optical isomers (enantiomers) are mirror images that cannot be superimposed; such a complex is chiral. Rotating a complex never makes a new isomer.

Isomers can be turned into each other only by breaking bonds and rebuilding them in new positions. Turning a model in space keeps every ligand next to the same neighbors, so it is the same complex seen from another side. In a square or an octahedron, two positions can be adjacent or opposite, so two like ligands give cis and trans. In a tetrahedron every pair of corners is adjacent, so $\mathrm{MA_2B_2}$ has only one form. A complex with no mirror plane, such as $\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}$, a three-bladed propeller, has a left-handed and a right-handed form.

blocks.html: Why is copper sulfate blue and zinc sulfate colorless? Why are some iron complexes attracted to a magnet and others not? Crystal field theory answers both. It builds on coordination compounds, orbital diagrams and light energy.

In an octahedral complex, the ligands raise the energy of the two d orbitals that point at them ($e_g$) above the other three ($t_{2g}$), by the splitting energy $\Delta_o$. Strong-field ligands give a large $\Delta_o$ (electrons pair up in $t_{2g}$ first: low spin); weak-field ligands give a small one (electrons spread out first: high spin). Absorbing light of energy $\Delta_o$ lifts an electron across the gap, and the complex shows the complementary color of the light absorbed.

The ligands' lone pairs act like negative charges. The $d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals point straight at the six ligands on the axes, so electrons in them are repelled more; the $d_{xy}$, $d_{xz}$ and $d_{yz}$ orbitals point between the ligands. Whether a fourth electron pairs in $t_{2g}$ or climbs to $e_g$ depends on which costs less: the pairing energy or $\Delta_o$. White light minus the absorbed color is what reaches your eye.

The order of ligands by $\Delta_o$, measured from absorption spectra, is the spectrochemical series. From weakest to strongest field: $\mathrm{I^-}$, $\mathrm{Br^-}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{F^-}$, $\mathrm{OH^-}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, en, $\mathrm{CN^-}$, CO.

blocks.title: Same ion, different ligands
blocks.q: How many unpaired electrons are in $\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}$ and in $\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}$?
steps: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$: iron is in group 8 and has lost two electrons, leaving $d^6$.
Water is weak-field: high spin, one electron in each of the five orbitals, then the sixth pairs in $t_{2g}$: $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$, 4 unpaired.
Cyanide is strong-field: low spin, all six pair in $t_{2g}$: $t_{2g}^6$, 0 unpaired. $\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}$ is diamagnetic.

blocks.q: $\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}$ absorbs most strongly near $500\ \text{nm}$. Find $\Delta_o$ in kJ/mol and predict its color.
steps: It absorbs green-yellow light, so it looks the complementary color: violet-purple.

items: $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions ($\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}$, $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$) have no electron that can jump the gap, so their compounds are usually colorless.
Tetrahedral complexes have a smaller splitting (about 4/9 of $\Delta_o$) and are nearly always high spin.
Paramagnetic (attracted by a magnet) means at least one unpaired electron; diamagnetic means none.
